title: A sequence in prose is invisible to every mechanical check, and a phrase can go stale without its number changing - the wrong half travels attached to a figure you did just measure, which is what makes it invisible
statement: A sequence in prose is invisible to every mechanical check - an id-and-status pass sees ids and statuses, never an ordinal. And a phrase can go stale without its number changing: "nine families" was carried whole out of an older sentence with only the figure in front of it refreshed, so the false half travelled attached to a number I had genuinely just measured - which is exactly what made it invisible.
context: 2026-08-23, preparing the durable kickoff prompt for a fresh session. THE FIRST HALF: the file's own section counting the times it has carried a stale statement had TWO different findings, added by two different commits, both labelled THE THIRTEENTH - so its counter was a whole occasion short and there was no fourteenth at all. A mechanical pass over 190 identifiers ran clean straight past it, because an ordinal is not an identifier and no gate has an opinion about a numbering. THE SECOND HALF happened inside the repair. Writing up that finding, I asserted the 190 identifiers spanned 'nine families'. Nothing had measured that; the phrase came whole out of the same file's TENTH entry - '68 across nine families' - with only the figure in front of it refreshed. Measured, it is fifteen. It reached three durable places including a pushed commit message that cannot be amended, and it sat INSIDE the sentence asserting the mechanical pass had run clean. An independent review pass caught it, not me and not any gate. PE-593 carried it; PE-595 corrects it.
recommendation: Treat the WORDS around a number as unverified until you have measured them too, especially when you have just measured the number - that freshness is what launders the rest of the sentence. When reusing a sentence's shape from anywhere, re-derive every claim in it rather than refreshing the figures, because the shape is where the stale part hides. And when a durable artifact carries an ordered sequence - numbered findings, versioned entries, a lettered ladder - check the sequence itself for gaps and collisions, since no foreign-key check, id sweep or status pass will ever look at it.
rationale: This project's controls are strong at exactly one thing: identifiers and their statuses. Every instrument it has built - G-IDS, the entity index, the id-and-status sweep - answers 'does this id exist and is its status what you said'. Prose sits outside all of them, and the parts of prose that look most like data are the parts that get least scrutiny, because a number reads as though something produced it. An ordinal and a carried phrase are both prose wearing the costume of a measured fact.
impact_if_followed: The half of a durable artifact that no gate can see gets read as deliberately as the half that gates check, and sequences stay countable. The cheap tell is available every time: if a clause would survive being deleted without changing the claim, it was never load-bearing and should not be there; if it would not, it needs measuring in the same breath as the number beside it.
impact_if_ignored: A false clause rides into a commit message on the back of a true number and cannot be amended afterwards, which is how this one escaped. Worse, it lands preferentially in the sentences that assert a check ran clean - so the artifact's own claim to have been verified is the place least likely to have been.

title: When an instrument changes and the numbers get worse, 'the new instrument is broken' and 'the old instrument was lying' produce identical evidence - only reading the disputed measurement by hand separates them
statement: A tool upgrade that makes measurements worse is ambiguous in a way that feels resolved but is not. The new instrument may be miscounting, or the old one may have been crediting things it should not have - and BOTH hypotheses predict exactly the same observation: numbers dropped, code unchanged. Trap 2 says a measurement that indicts known-good code is measuring itself, and that heuristic is correct and useful; but it has a converse that must be checked before it is applied, because sometimes the code was not as good as the old measurement said. The discriminator is always the same and it is cheap: shrink the disagreement down to ONE artefact small enough to adjudicate by hand, get both instruments' detailed output for it, and read the disputed item yourself.
context: 2026-08-23. Upgrading @vitest/coverage-v8 from 3.2.6 to 4.1.11 dropped about twenty files below ADR-0016's 95% line threshold while every test still passed and no source file changed. It read exactly like a broken instrument, and the deferred-work row filed for it said so. The experiment: same source, same test file, same three passing tests, coverage under v3 then v4, over a 55-line component chosen because it could be counted by hand. v3 reported 100% lines and nothing uncovered; v4 reported 90% and named exactly one line. That line held a Button whose onClick was an inline arrow; the tests rendered it but never clicked it. BOTH providers' function maps recorded the same uncalled function - they differed only in whether an uninvoked callback makes its LINE uncovered. Since the gate is lines-only by explicit design, v3 had been rendering every untested inline handler invisible to it. The twenty files were never properly covered.
recommendation: Before concluding that a new instrument is wrong, find the smallest artefact on which the two instruments disagree, obtain each one's detailed per-item output rather than its summary percentage, and adjudicate the disputed item by reading the code. Prefer an artefact you can count by hand over a representative one. If both instruments turn out to AGREE on the underlying facts and differ only in how they aggregate them, the question is not which is correct in general but which aggregation matches what the gate claims to measure - and that is answerable from the gate's own definition.
rationale: The two hypotheses are observationally identical at the summary level, which is the only level anyone normally looks at. A percentage cannot distinguish 'wrongly counted' from 'previously miscredited'. Detailed output can, because instruments usually agree about raw execution and disagree about attribution - and attribution is checkable against the code.
impact_if_followed: A tool upgrade that exposes a real gap gets treated as the discovery it is, and the gap gets closed. Governance thresholds keep meaning what they say, because the question 'which aggregation matches the gate's own definition' gets asked out loud instead of settled by whichever number is more convenient.
impact_if_ignored: The comfortable reading wins, because it is also the cheaper one: the new tool is blamed, the upgrade is refused or the threshold is quietly lowered, and code that has never been executed by any test keeps counting as covered. The register then records a number that is true about the measurement and false about the software.

title: Two runners exercising one shared artefact are ONE instrument for locating a fault and TWO for verifying its repair - LL-009 applies to the shared component, not to the harnesses around it
statement: LL-009 says two instruments agreeing is one instrument when they share a mechanism. The trap in applying it is that superficial difference feels like independence: a different test runner, a different orchestrator, a different machine. None of that is independence if both paths build or load the SAME artefact - the thing under test is identical and only the scaffolding differs. But the relationship is asymmetric, and the second half is worth as much as the first: the very same pair of observations that is WEAK evidence about WHERE a fault lives is STRONG evidence that a change to their shared component WORKED. Independence matters for localising a cause. It matters much less for verifying a repair to the thing they share.
context: 2026-08-23. A dependency bump of the SQL Server base image failed under Testcontainers and, identically, under docker-compose. I read two execution paths agreeing as independent corroboration and concluded the fault was in the vendor's image, recording that production must not move to that version. Both paths build the project's own Dockerfile. The vendor images were fine - ldd reported nothing missing in either - and the real cause was a hardcoded package-repo URL in that shared Dockerfile, which installed a package built for the old base onto the new one. I had quoted LL-009 earlier in the same session before walking into it. When the coupled fix landed, those same two paths both went green, and that confirmation was worth MORE than the failure had been, because the change was made in the component they both exercise.
recommendation: Before calling two failing observations independent corroboration, ask what artefact each one actually loads, not what tooling drives it. If the answer is the same file, the same image or the same build, you have one observation twice and you have learned nothing about where the fault is. Conversely, once you have changed that shared artefact, those same two paths are a good verification precisely because they both depend on it - so do not discount a repair's confirmation on the grounds that the observers were not independent.
rationale: Independence is a property of what is being measured, not of who is measuring. Two harnesses over one artefact vary everything except the variable that matters. The asymmetry follows: for localisation you need observations that could have differed, and these could not; for verification you need observations that would have failed if the change did not work, and these would.
impact_if_followed: Fault localisation stops being decided by a coincidence of tooling, and repairs to shared components get the credit their confirmation deserves. A wrong conclusion about where a fault lives - the kind that reaches a production recommendation - gets caught before it is recorded.
impact_if_ignored: A shared artefact's defect gets attributed to whatever lies beyond it, most often a vendor, and the resulting statement is both wrong and expensive: it forecloses an upgrade that was never the problem, and it leaves the real coupling in place to fire again on the next bump.

title: A pinned base image and a pinned package repository are ONE decision expressed in two places, and only one of them is automated - so an automated bump can never go green alone
statement: Where a Dockerfile pins a base image AND separately configures a package repository whose URL encodes the same platform - a distribution release, a product major, an architecture - those two lines are a single decision written twice. Dependency bots update the one they understand and cannot see the other, so their pull request installs packages built for the old platform onto the new one and fails in ways that look like the vendor's fault. The general form is broader than containers: any pair of version-bearing values that must agree, where only one has an automated updater, will drift the first time the updater runs. The fix is not to distrust the bot; it is to put the coupling where the next person editing either line will read it, because a register entry is a record and a comment beside the line is a control.
context: 2026-08-23. A Dependabot pull request bumped a SQL Server base image from one major to the next, changing only the FROM line. The Dockerfile installs full-text search - required by the product's search requirements and carrying a language-specific word-breaker - from a hardcoded repository URL naming the OLD distribution release and the OLD product major. That package pulls in the database server itself, so the bump installed the old platform's server binary over the new image's own, leaving a binary linked against a library the new base does not ship. The pull request had been open five weeks and could never have gone green. The fix moved both lines together and added a comment above them saying they are one decision.
recommendation: When a build file pins a base image, grep the same file for any other line carrying a distribution release, a product major or an architecture, and treat every such pair as one decision. Write the coupling as a comment immediately above the lines rather than only into a tracking row. When a bot's bump of one of them fails, check the pair before concluding anything about the upstream artefact.
rationale: Automated updaters operate on the syntax they were built to recognise, not on the semantics of the file. A FROM line is recognisable; a version embedded in a URL is not. The asymmetry is structural and will not be fixed by the bot, so it has to be absorbed by whoever reads the file - which means the warning has to live where they are already looking.
impact_if_followed: A base-image bump either lands complete or fails for a reason that is immediately legible, and the next person to edit either line is told about the other by the file itself rather than by a register they may never open.
impact_if_ignored: The bot's pull request sits red indefinitely and is eventually dismissed as an upstream problem, which is both wrong and costly: it blocks a platform upgrade that was always available, and the diagnosis lands on a vendor who did nothing wrong.

title: A CORRECTED MEASUREMENT DOES NOT CORRECT THE INFERENCE SOMEBODY BUILT ON IT
statement: When a wrong number is fixed, the CONCLUSIONS drawn from it while it was wrong do not travel with the fix. They stay where they were written, now detached from the evidence that produced them, and they read exactly like conclusions drawn from the corrected number. Fixing a measurement is therefore only half the repair: the other half is finding what was inferred from the old value and re-deriving it.
context: DW-082. Version one of the coverage triage script scraped vitest's ASCII table and misread TopBar's compressed 'Uncovered Line #s' cell of '92-138' as a 47-line range; the structured data says seven lines. From that wrong size an explanation was reasoned out - that TopBar's cause could not be untested handlers, and must instead be the DevRoleSwitcher coverage-exclusion asymmetry charging TopBar for a branch the exclusion hides. Version two of the script corrected the NUMBER to seven. Nobody re-derived the CAUSE. The wrong explanation then travelled into PE-610, into PE-611, into prm-next.md's next-action block, and into the memory index as a standing warning that this file 'is NOT a handler fix; it needs its own decision'. Measured on 2026-08-25: all seven of TopBar's uncovered lines are ordinary inline handlers, the lazy() declaration records three hits, and the call site has no statement starting on it, so it never enters the line metric at all. The exclusion charges TopBar nothing.
recommendation: When you correct a measurement, immediately search for what was CONCLUDED from the old one - in your own notes, in the register, in any prompt or handoff - and re-derive each conclusion from the new value rather than assuming the fix propagated. Treat the correction as incomplete until that sweep is done. Where a conclusion cannot be cheaply re-derived, mark it as resting on a superseded measurement rather than leaving it standing.
rationale: A stale NUMBER is at least in tension with the world and can be caught by re-measuring. A stale INFERENCE is well-formed prose that no gate, no id-and-status pass and no re-measurement can see, because the number it depended on is no longer present in it. It has also, by then, usually been summarised once or twice - and each summary strips the provenance that would let a reader notice it was built on something withdrawn. In this instance the wrong inference was on its way to costing an operator interview for a decision that did not exist.
impact_if_followed: A corrected measurement closes out completely, and downstream artifacts stop carrying explanations whose evidence has been withdrawn.
impact_if_ignored: Withdrawn evidence keeps producing live instructions. Sessions act on a cause that was never real - scheduling ceremonies, asking for decisions, or avoiding work - and the mechanical checks all pass, because an ordinal, an instruction and a causal claim are invisible to every one of them.

title: A COMMAND CHAIN FAILS CLOSED FOR THE COMMAND THAT BREAKS AND OPEN FOR EVERY COMMAND THAT READS A FILE THE CHAIN WAS SUPPOSED TO WRITE
statement: In `A && B && C`, a failure in A stops the chain - but only for the commands that RUN. Any later command that would have consumed A's output can still succeed on a stale copy of that output left behind by an earlier, unrelated run. The guard protects sequencing, not freshness, and a shared scratch directory silently supplies the missing input.
context: DW-082, 2026-08-25. The chain was `git add src/Acmp.Web && cat > /tmp/c4.txt <<EOF ... EOF && git commit -F /tmp/c4.txt`. The `git add` failed because the shell's working directory was already inside src/Acmp.Web, so the heredoc that writes the commit message NEVER RAN. A later invocation from the repo root then re-ran the commit step against /tmp/c4.txt - which existed, left over from an unrelated session on 2026-08-19 - and git committed the correct FILES under a commit message describing a different feature on a different branch. Nothing errored. The commit was found only by reading `git log` afterwards and noticing the subject was somebody else's commit summary.
recommendation: Write generated inputs to a path unique to the run - `/tmp/name-$$.txt` or a session directory - and delete it after use, so a stale copy cannot be adopted. Where a command consumes a file another step was supposed to produce, either generate and consume it in ONE command, or assert the file's freshness before reading it. And read back what a write-then-consume chain actually produced: `git log -1 --format=%s` costs nothing.
rationale: The failure mode is invisible precisely because every individual command behaved correctly. `git commit -F` cannot know the file it was handed is not the file the author meant; it has no way to distinguish a stale artifact from a fresh one. Commit messages are also unamendable once pushed, which is why this project already counts assertions that escaped into them - and a message describing unrelated work is worse than a vague one, because it will be believed.
impact_if_followed: A broken chain produces no commit rather than a confidently mislabelled one, and the durable record says what actually happened.
impact_if_ignored: Shared scratch paths turn a broken pipeline into a plausible-looking result. In git specifically, the wrong text becomes permanent the moment it is pushed.

title: WHEN YOU WRAP AN EXISTING FAILURE TO MAKE IT LEGIBLE, THE FAILURE IS NOT YOURS - ONLY THE MESSAGE IS. ANY ASSERTION THAT WOULD STILL HOLD AGAINST THE UNWRAPPED ORIGINAL IS TESTING THE FRAMEWORK, NOT YOUR CHANGE
statement:
A whole class of work here does not CREATE a failure, it IMPROVES one that already happens: a timeout that already fires but says nothing useful, an exception that already throws but names no context, an error already logged without the identifier that would let anyone act on it. For that class, the failing behaviour is inherited and the DIFFERENCE is the entire deliverable - so the test must assert the difference. An assertion that would pass identically against the un-improved original is asserting the framework's behaviour and reporting it as proof of yours.

THE INSTANCE (`DW-084`, PR `#309`, 2026-08-25). The change wraps a Testcontainers container start in a `CancellationTokenSource` so a hung container fails fast with the container's own log attached, instead of being retried until the CI job hits its 25-minute ceiling and reports `cancelled` - a verdict that is neither pass nor fail. The forcing test asserted three things: that a `TimeoutException` is thrown, that its message names the bound, and that it carries a marker the container printed. Mutating the wrapper away - rethrowing the raw exception - showed that Testcontainers ALREADY throws `TimeoutException`, carrying the message 'The operation has timed out.'. The type assertion had been inherited from the framework all along and would have gone green with the entire guard deleted.

WHY IT IS NOT COVERED BY `LL-013`, and the distinction is exact rather than pedantic. `LL-013` is about a mutant that PASSES: proof of nothing, because a missing test, a stale build and an uncovered branch all look identical. Here the mutant FAILED - the self-proving direction - and the check worked. What the failure revealed was not a missing detector but a MIS-ATTRIBUTED one: an assertion that was live, load-bearing in appearance, and satisfied by code nobody in this repository wrote. `LL-013` asks whether the detector exists. This asks whose behaviour the detector is detecting.

WHY IT IS EASY TO MISS. Asserting on an exception TYPE reads as more rigorous than asserting on a message - types are structural, messages are brittle prose - so the instinct that produces the vacuous assertion is the same instinct that usually produces a good one. And the type assertion is not wrong, merely inherited: it will never fail spuriously, which is exactly why it will never fail usefully either.
context: DW-084 / DEC-077 d4/d5, 2026-08-25. The row required proof by FORCING the failure rather than by a green run, because the hang it guards against is intermittent. Forcing it produced a passing test; mutating the guard away is what showed one of that test's three assertions was inherited from Testcontainers rather than earned by the change.
recommendation: Before believing a test over a make-it-better change, ask what the code did BEFORE and delete the improvement in a scratch mutation. Every assertion that still passes is measuring the pre-existing behaviour and must be treated as scaffolding, not evidence. Keep those assertions if they document intent, but never cite them as the proof. Then name the delta in words - 'the message now carries the container name, the bound, and the log' - and write one assertion per clause of that sentence. In practice this means preferring an assertion on the ADDED CONTENT (a marker, an identifier, a bound) over an assertion on the failure's shape, precisely when the failure's shape was not yours to begin with.
rationale: Improving a diagnostic is one of the few changes where the observable being asserted on existed before the change did. Everywhere else, the thing under test would not happen at all without the code being tested, so a type-or-shape assertion is automatically discriminating. That structural difference is invisible at the point of writing the test - the test looks like every other test - and the mutation is the only cheap thing that exposes it.
impact_if_followed: A guard added to make a failure legible is proven by the legibility it added, so deleting the guard reddens the suite. The test keeps its value when the framework's own behaviour changes underneath it.
impact_if_ignored: A test that would pass with the entire change reverted is filed as evidence that the change works. The guard can then be lost in a refactor or a dependency upgrade with the suite staying green - the silent-loss shape this project already treats as the most expensive kind.

title: A GENERATOR THAT GUARANTEES THE QUOTED RECORDS SAYS NOTHING ABOUT THE PROSE AROUND THEM - AND THE PROSE IS WHAT FRAMES THE QUESTION THE OPERATOR ANSWERS
statement:
`LL-011` fixed a real failure: an artifact the operator reads to DECIDE must carry each cited record's own text, quoted from the canonical store by a generator rather than paraphrased. The remediation works, and it is now mechanical - a docket generator prints every field and a verifier confirms byte-identity before publishing.

BUT THE GUARANTEE HAS A BOUNDARY NOBODY DREW. It covers the QUOTED BLOCKS. It says nothing about the agent's connective prose - the paragraph introducing each question, the recommendation, the trade-off, the sentence explaining why an option is expensive. That prose is unverified by construction, and it is the part the operator actually reasons over: the records supply the facts, the framing supplies the QUESTION.

THE INSTANCE (`DW-085`, 2026-08-26). A docket carried fifteen fields across four records, every one verified byte-identical, and the verifier was itself calibrated with two injected faults. Around those verified blocks sat a framing paragraph asserting the work *"could not meet this project's prove-by-forcing bar without committing a deliberately-hanging Dockerfile"* - and that its evidence would therefore be weaker. **It was false and had never been measured.** A Dockerfile written to a temp directory at run time forces the build perfectly well and ships nothing; the objection was to OWNING the artifact, and the objection was allowed to swallow the technique. The false constraint partly justified the agent's recommendation to carry the row. The operator overrode it and the outcome was unaffected - which is luck, not process.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE SAME ERROR IN A NOTE. A wrong sentence in a progress entry is read later, by someone with the register open, in a context where checking is cheap. A wrong sentence in a decision slate is read AT THE MOMENT OF DECIDING, by the one person who cannot check it, and it is load-bearing precisely then. The `LL-011` machinery makes the surrounding prose look MORE trustworthy, not less, because everything beside it is provably exact.
context: DW-085 / DEC-078, 2026-08-26. Found by attempting the thing the slate had declared impossible, immediately after the interview that slate was built for - the forced test passed on the first attempt and took exactly its bound.
recommendation: Mark the two kinds of content apart, and hold them to different standards on purpose. QUOTED blocks are generated and verified; CONNECTIVE prose is the agent's own claim and must be labelled as such where it appears - 'my reading', 'my recommendation', 'not measured'. Then apply one rule to the connective half: any sentence asserting that something CANNOT be done, or that an option is expensive or blocked, must name the attempt that established it or say plainly that no attempt was made. 'Cannot' is a claim about every method, and it is the cheapest sentence to write and the dearest to justify - so before it goes in front of the operator, either try the thing or downgrade the wording to 'I have not found a way'.
rationale: The failure is structural rather than careless. A verification mechanism raises confidence in everything NEAR it, including what it does not check, because the reader has no way to see where the guarantee stops. That is the same asymmetry `LL-011` itself identified from the other side - an identifier reads as precision to the person who can resolve it and as an obstacle to the person who cannot - and it reappears here one level up: verified quotation reads as rigour across the whole page, to a reader who cannot see which half was verified.
impact_if_followed: The operator can see which sentences are generated fact and which are the agent's unverified reading, and every blocked-or-impossible claim in a decision slate is either tested or openly marked as untested.
impact_if_ignored: Decision slates keep getting more rigorous in their quoted half while the framing half stays unchecked - and the framing half is the one that decides what is asked. An unmeasured 'cannot' can remove a real option from the operator's list without either party noticing it was removed.

title: WRITING CODE INTO A FILE THROUGH ANOTHER LANGUAGE SILENTLY EATS ITS ESCAPES, AND THE RESULT STILL LOOKS PLAUSIBLE - SO PROVE GENERATED CODE RUNS, NEVER READ IT AND BELIEVE IT
statement:
When a script generates source for another file - a Python heredoc writing TypeScript, a shell heredoc writing a Dockerfile, any generator emitting code - every escape sequence passes through TWO levels of interpretation, and the outer one usually wins silently. `'\\n'` in a Python string becomes a real newline in the output file, not the two characters a JS or regex literal needs. The generated file then contains a string split across two lines, or a character class broken in half.

WHAT MAKES IT EXPENSIVE IS THAT THE DAMAGE LOOKS FINE. The output is still readable, still nearly right, and a `grep` for the surrounding text still matches. The failure surfaces later as a parse error in a test run, or - worse - as a snippet embedded in documentation that nobody executes until the session that needs it.

FOUR OCCURRENCES IN ONE SESSION, 2026-08-26, each costing a cycle. (1) A Dockerfile written for a forced-build test: `FROM alpine:3.20\\nRUN sleep 30` became two source lines and the C# would not compile. (2) A test fixture: multi-line document bodies became unterminated string literals, and the whole test FILE failed to load - reported as 59 passing tests and one failed file, which reads like a test failure and is not. (3) and (4) A regex embedded in a markdown code block, twice: the character class `[^.\\n]` split across two lines, producing a snippet that would have failed for whoever copied it.

THE ASYMMETRY WITH ORDINARY TYPOS. A typo in code you write directly fails at the point you wrote it. A mangled escape in code you GENERATE fails at the point someone else runs it, which may be a different session, and the generator that produced it has usually been thrown away by then.
context:
WBS-24.2 / WBS-24.3 / DW-084, 2026-08-26. Found by hitting it four separate times in one session; the fourth was inside the pre-handoff pass whose whole purpose is catching things a fresh session would trip over - which is where it would have done the most damage, because the reader would have copied a broken snippet out of the resume.

A FIFTH OCCURRENCE, WBS-24.4, LATER THE SAME DAY - AND IT IS THE ONE THAT ARGUES HARDEST FOR THE RULE, because it happened to an agent who had just written this lesson down. A bash heredoc quoted `<<'EOF'`, the form believed to be literal, was used to write a Node scanner containing a path-separator regex. One backslash level was eaten anyway: the file arrived with the escape missing and Node refused to parse it. It cost only minutes BECAUSE the very next action happened to be running the generated script - the recommendation below, applied by accident rather than by discipline.

WHAT THE FIFTH ADDS THAT THE FIRST FOUR DID NOT. The first four are one shape: an outer language interpreting an escape meant for the inner one. The fifth shows that KNOWING THIS, AND HAVING JUST WRITTEN IT DOWN, DOES NOT PREVENT IT - and that the quoting form assumed safe was not. So the defence cannot be vigilance, or a remembered rule about which heredoc is literal; it has to be the mechanical one: run the thing. In this instance the better remedy was also simpler than the rule suggests - the file was rewritten with the editor tool instead of through a heredoc, REMOVING THE SECOND INTERPRETATION LAYER ENTIRELY rather than trying to escape correctly through it.
recommendation: Build the escape explicitly rather than trusting it through a layer: `chr(92) + 'n'` in Python, or a placeholder token substituted afterwards. Then - and this is the part that actually catches it - PROVE THE GENERATED CODE RUNS. Extract the block and execute it, compile the file, or run the test that loads it, in the same breath as writing it. Reading the output and finding it plausible is exactly the check that fails here, because plausible is what the damage looks like. For a snippet embedded in prose, where nothing compiles it, extraction-and-execution is the ONLY check there is.
rationale: Escape mangling is invisible to every instrument this project already trusts. A gate compiles committed source, not a heredoc's intent; an id-and-status pass reads identifiers, not string literals; and a snippet inside a markdown fence is not code to any tool in the repository. The generator is also usually a throwaway, so there is no artefact left to re-inspect when the breakage is noticed. The only moment the fault is cheap to catch is immediately after generation, and only by execution.
impact_if_followed: Generated code either runs or fails in the session that produced it, while the generator still exists and the intent is still in hand.
impact_if_ignored: Mangled escapes ship inside test fixtures, Dockerfiles and documentation snippets, and surface as parse errors or broken copy-paste in a later session that has no idea a generator was involved.

title: A plan row can be a FAITHFUL quotation of a clause an ADR has already superseded - and when an ADR names the rows it will amend, that list is the instrument
statement: A work row that quotes its requirement accurately can still be wrong, because the REQUIREMENT is what a decision superseded. Nothing mechanical can see it: the ids resolve, the statuses are right, the trace gate passes, and the registers agree with each other - they simply agree about a sentence that a decision overruled. So sweep the ADR and DECISION registers before sizing, not only the requirement register. And where an ADR names the rows it undertook to amend, TREAT THAT LIST AS A CHECKLIST and compare it against every row that quotes the ADR's subject: the row the follow-through missed is the one still asserting the superseded text.
context:
WBS-24.6 (DW-035 / FR-154), 2026-08-27, before any code was written. The WBS item, the deferred-work row and the requirement all said the audit-log export is *"accessible only to Auditor and Administrator"*. ADR-0027 (Approved) decides that audit read, search, EXPORT and delete are {Auditor, Chairman, Secretary} with Administrator EXCLUDED on segregation-of-duties grounds, and it names exporting explicitly. Building to the row's own text would have reversed an Approved ADR and broken control C-INS-03 - trap 32's shape, but arriving through a row that was not careless: it was a correct citation.

WHY EVERY INSTRUMENT PASSED. count-prompt-ids.py resolved all 271 cited identifiers and read every status correctly. The inline prose-status checker found nothing. G-TRACE passed. The requirement register was internally consistent. The fault is not a dangling id, a wrong status, or a missing link - it is a true sentence whose source died.

WHAT ACTUALLY CLOSED IT. Trap 32 / LL-008 got me into the ADR register, but that alone only produces a candidate. ADR-0027's own text records its follow-through: it states that FR-151 and FR-153 will carry a pointer to it. Both do, as relates_to edges. FR-154 had neither the pointer nor the edge - it was a Phase-2 requirement when the ADR was written and was simply missed. The ADR's promise about itself was the discriminator, and it is cheap to check.

The code had implemented the ADR correctly on both sides for months (Policies.AuditRead and the App.tsx route gate); only the register was out of step. DEC-081 d2 and SC-036 reconciled it before any code was written.
recommendation: Before sizing a work item, read the ADR and DECISION registers for the row's subject as well as the requirement register (LL-008, trap 32). Then, for every ADR that turns out to govern it, read the ADR's OWN text for a list of rows it said it would amend or annotate - and check each one actually carries the pointer or the trace edge. Any row on that list without it is still asserting the superseded text, and any row NOT on that list that quotes the same subject was never considered at all.
rationale: The failure mode is invisible to every mechanical control this package has, because none of them compares a requirement's text against a decision that overruled it - they check identifiers, statuses and link existence, all of which are correct here. The ADR's own follow-through list is the only artifact that already names the affected set, so it converts an open-ended 'read everything' sweep into a finite checklist.
impact_if_followed: A row whose requirement clause is dead is caught during sizing, before code is written, at the cost of reading one ADR. Here that prevented building an authorization surface that would have reversed an Approved ADR and defeated a segregation-of-duties control on the audit log - the one dataset whose access rules exist to constrain the platform's own operator.
impact_if_ignored: The build follows a row that reads correct, cites correctly, and passes every gate, while silently reversing a settled architectural decision. Nothing reports it: the code and the register would then agree with each other and both disagree with the ADR, which is the configuration hardest to detect later because the disagreement has no witness.

title: A test that asserts an ABSENCE straight after a framework lifecycle call is asserting against work the framework may not have done yet - and a runtime upgrade can empty it silently, because a negative assertion is true over an empty execution.
statement: When a test invokes a framework lifecycle method and asserts immediately afterwards, it is asserting against work the framework has not promised to have finished. If the assertion is NEGATIVE - nothing was received, nothing threw, no rows were written - it holds identically whether the code under test ran and correctly did nothing, or never ran at all. Which of those is happening is decided by the framework's scheduling, an implementation detail that changes between versions, so the test can be emptied by an upgrade while still passing. Only an instrument that measures EXECUTION rather than OUTCOME can tell the two apart.
context: The `net8.0` to `net10.0` migration, `DW-080` phase A, 2026-08-28 (`DEF-113`). `WebexWebhookRegistrarTests` called `IHostedService.StartAsync` and then asserted `api.DidNotReceiveWithAnyArgs()`. .NET 10's documented breaking change *BackgroundService runs all of ExecuteAsync as a Task* moved the whole method body onto a background thread, where .NET 8 had run everything before the first await inline on the caller. `ExecuteTask` read `WaitingForActivation` with no exception; a positive assertion in the same place failed with *"Actually received no matching calls"*. The test passed on BOTH runtimes and the suite was 1167 green either way. The sole signal was the per-file coverage floor putting the file at 92.00% (23/25) - two lines of a three-line method - which reads exactly like an attribution artefact and invites an exclusion or a lower threshold, either of which deletes the evidence.
recommendation: Join deterministically before asserting, and note that NEITHER lifecycle method is a join: `StartAsync` returns with the body still pending, and `StopAsync` cancels the stopping token BEFORE it awaits - so on a loaded runner it can cancel the work before the thread pool starts it and then join a task that did nothing. Await `ExecuteTask` itself: it IS the running body, no cancellation is involved, so it is deterministic by construction rather than by timing. Then assert the POSITIVE observable the path produces rather than the absence of one, so the assertion has something to be false about. And when a per-file coverage floor names lines inside a method whose test passes, get the LINE NUMBERS and read them before concluding the instrument is miscounting - the hit COUNTS on the surrounding lines usually adjudicate on their own, by accounting exactly for the callers you can name.
rationale: A negative assertion carries no information about whether the code executed, because it is satisfied by the empty run. The test suite therefore cannot distinguish a correct no-op from a no-op that never started, and no amount of adding assertions of the same shape will fix that. Coverage is the only routine instrument that measures execution rather than outcome, which is exactly why a per-file floor discriminated where 1167 passing tests could not - and why the two remedies the number invites, an exclusion or a lower threshold, would have removed the only working signal while leaving the vacuous test in place.
impact_if_followed: The lifecycle path is proven to run, and a future runtime upgrade that changes scheduling fails loudly at an assertion instead of quietly emptying the test. The coverage floor keeps its power to detect the class.
impact_if_ignored: A framework upgrade converts a passing test into one that exercises nothing, and the only evidence is a coverage figure that looks like an artefact of the new toolchain - so the cheapest-looking fix suppresses the measurement and enshrines the empty test permanently.

title: A valid argument resting on a WEAK premise is weakened, not strengthened, by a stronger premise you did not check - and the unnecessary sentence is the one that reads as rigorous.
statement: When an argument is already sound on a premise that is trivially true, adding a stronger-sounding premise that has not been measured does not make it more convincing - it inserts the only falsifiable claim in the whole argument, and puts it in the sentence a reader is least likely to challenge, because it is the one that sounds like it came from evidence. The word to distrust in your own prose is ONLY: `the ONLY project`, `the ONLY join`, `the ONLY place`. It is a claim about an entire set, it is almost never what the argument needs, and it is nearly always cheaper to delete than to verify.
context: DW-080 phase A, 2026-08-28 (`DEF-113`), twice in one session. (a) Establishing which lines a CI coverage gate meant, the argument needed only that the local test set is a SUBSET of CI's - trivially true, and enough, since coverage is monotone in tests executed and equal counts then force set identity. Written up, it acquired *"`Acmp.Application.Tests` is the ONLY project whose tests reach this file"*, which was never measured and is false; `Acmp.Api.Tests` reaches it too. (b) An hour later the fix's write-up called `StopAsync` *"the only deterministic join"*. Also unmeasured, also false - it cancels the stopping token before awaiting - and CI rejected the fix built on it. Both sentences reached a pushed commit message, which cannot be amended. In (a) the conclusion survived untouched because the extra premise was load-bearing for nothing; in (b) it did not.
recommendation: Before writing a durable artifact, identify the WEAKEST premise the argument actually needs and state that one. Then treat every remaining `only`, `never`, `always`, `cannot` and `the single` in your own draft as a measurement request: either run the command that settles it in the same breath, or strike the word. A sentence that can be deleted without weakening the conclusion should be deleted rather than verified - it is pure liability, since it can only ever be wrong.
rationale: An unnecessary premise carries all of the risk and none of the load. It cannot strengthen a conclusion that already follows, but it can be false, and when it is, it discredits the surrounding reasoning that was in fact correct - or, worse, it is load-bearing for the NEXT decision, where nobody re-checks it because it arrived attached to an argument that was verified. Universal claims are the common form because they read as thoroughness, and thoroughness is exactly what a reader declines to re-derive.
impact_if_followed: Durable artifacts carry the premises their conclusions actually rest on, so a reader who checks one sentence checks the one that matters, and the register keeps its authority when a claim does turn out wrong.
impact_if_ignored: An unmeasured universal ships inside a verified argument, inherits its credibility, and is later reused as an established fact by a session that has no reason to doubt it - and it reaches commit messages, which cannot be amended.

title: THE QUOTED RECORDS ARE GUARANTEED AND YOUR PROSE AROUND THEM IS NOT - AND THE PREMISE THE ARGUMENT DID NOT NEED IS THE ONE THAT WILL BE FALSE. Merged from `LL-023` and `LL-027` by operator instruction, 2026-08-28.
statement:
`LL-011`'s remedy works and is mechanical: a generator prints every cited record from the canonical store and a verifier confirms byte-identity before publishing. THE GUARANTEE STOPS AT THE QUOTED BLOCKS. The connective prose - the paragraph introducing a question, the recommendation, the trade-off, the sentence explaining why an option is expensive - is unverified by construction, and it is the half the reader actually reasons over: the records supply the FACTS, the framing supplies the QUESTION. Worse, the verification machinery makes that prose read as MORE trustworthy, not less, because everything beside it is provably exact.

THE UNVERIFIED HALF FAILS IN ONE PREDICTABLE WAY, AND NAMING IT IS WHAT MAKES THIS ACTIONABLE: an unnecessary universal. When an argument is already sound on a premise that is trivially true, a stronger-sounding premise adds no support whatsoever - it merely inserts the only falsifiable claim in the whole argument, and puts it in the sentence a reader is least likely to challenge, because it is the one that sounds like it came from evidence. The word to distrust in your own draft is ONLY; also NEVER and CANNOT. Each is a claim about an entire set, each is almost never what the argument needs, and each is far cheaper to delete than to verify.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE IN A SLATE THAN IN A NOTE. A wrong sentence in a progress entry is read later, by someone with the register open, where checking is cheap. A wrong sentence in a decision artifact is read AT THE MOMENT OF DECIDING, by the one person who cannot check it, and it is load-bearing precisely then.
context:
TWO INSTANCES, THREE DAYS APART, BOTH IN ARTIFACTS OR COMMITS THAT OUTLIVED THE SESSION.

`DW-085`, 2026-08-26. A docket carried fifteen fields across four records, every one verified byte-identical, the verifier itself calibrated with two injected faults. Around those verified blocks sat a framing paragraph asserting the work *"could not meet this project's prove-by-forcing bar without committing a deliberately-hanging Dockerfile"*. It was false and had never been measured: a Dockerfile written to a temp directory at run time forces the build perfectly well and ships nothing. The false constraint partly justified the recommendation to carry the row. The operator overrode it and the outcome was unaffected - which is luck, not process.

`DW-080` phase A, 2026-08-28 (`DEF-113`). Three unmeasured universals in one session, every one the word ONLY. (a) *"`Acmp.Application.Tests` is the ONLY project whose tests reach this file"* - false; `Acmp.Api.Tests` reaches it too. The set-identity argument needed only that the local tests are a SUBSET of CI's, which is trivially true, so the conclusion was untouched and the unnecessary premise was the sole false one. (b) *"`StopAsync` ... the only deterministic join"* - it is not a join at all, and CI rejected the fix built on it. (c) A confident *"Docker's layer cache"* cause for `DEF-114`, measured and discarded before filing when an identical rebuild took 33 seconds and a one-byte-different one 31. The first two reached a pushed commit message, which cannot be amended.
recommendation: 1. Mark the two kinds of content APART wherever the operator will read them, and hold them to different standards on purpose: quoted blocks are generated and verified, connective prose is the agent's own claim and must be labelled as such where it appears - `my reading`, `my recommendation`, `not measured`. 2. Treat every `only`, `never`, `cannot`, `always` and `the single` in your own draft as a MEASUREMENT REQUEST: run the command that settles it in the same breath, or strike the word. 3. Before writing a premise, identify the WEAKEST one the argument actually needs and state that one; a premise the conclusion does not need should be DELETED rather than verified, because it carries all of the risk and none of the load. 4. Any sentence asserting that something cannot be done, or that an option is blocked or expensive, must name the attempt that established it or say plainly that no attempt was made - `cannot` is a claim about every method, the cheapest sentence to write and the dearest to justify.
rationale: An unnecessary premise cannot strengthen a conclusion that already follows, but it can be false - and when it is, it discredits the surrounding reasoning that was in fact correct, or worse, is reused later as an established fact by a session that has no reason to doubt it, because it arrived attached to an argument that was verified. Universal claims are the common form precisely because they read as thoroughness, and thoroughness is the one thing a reader declines to re-derive. The generator closed the gap between the store and the page; this closes the gap between the page and the sentence that frames it.
impact_if_followed: The operator decides on claims that are either quoted from the store or visibly labelled as the agent's own, and the agent's own claims survive contact with a command. A decision artifact stops being trustworthy only in its verified half.
impact_if_ignored: A false constraint or an unmeasured universal rides inside a byte-verified artifact, inherits its credibility at the exact moment someone is deciding, and reaches commit messages that cannot be amended.

title: A REPRODUCTION THAT CHANGES TWO THINGS AT ONCE CONFIRMS WHICHEVER ONE YOU WERE ALREADY LOOKING AT - AND IT IS THE STRONGEST-FEELING EVIDENCE THERE IS, BECAUSE YOU MADE THE SYMPTOM COME BACK ON DEMAND.
statement:
Recreating a failure on demand feels like proof of its cause, and it is not. It is proof that SOMETHING in what you changed is sufficient to produce the symptom. If the step you took to set up the reproduction altered more than one thing, the reproduction cannot distinguish between them - and it will silently credit whichever one you were already watching, because that is the one you wrote down as the precondition.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES THIS DANGEROUS: a reproduction CONFIRMS, only an intervention EXPLAINS. Confirmation is cheap, satisfying, and available for every wrong hypothesis that happens to travel with a right one. The test that actually separates causes is to change ONE variable and predict the outcome BEFORE running it - and the most informative version of that is the fix, because a fix that fails under the true precondition falsifies the mechanism you built it on.
context:
`DEF-114`, 2026-08-28. `DW-085`'s forced-build guard failed locally and passed in CI. Hypothesis: Testcontainers skips a build when the named image already exists. To confirm it I pre-created the image and re-ran the single test; it failed identically in 804 ms. That was recorded as *"PROVEN by reproduction"* and written into the defect row, a progress entry, the resume, the memory index and THREE pushed commit messages, alongside an explicit statement that the rival explanation - Docker's layer cache - had been *"measured and DISCARDED"*.

**Pre-creating the image did two things: it created the named image, AND it warmed the `RUN sleep 30` layer in the build cache.** The cache was the real cause. The rival explanation had been dismissed on a 33-second identical rebuild measured minutes after the daemon started, with the cache cold - a true number about a state that no longer held. Warm, and under a brand-new tag, the same build takes about two seconds.

IT WAS CAUGHT ONLY BECAUSE THE FIX FAILED. A per-run image TAG was applied, the test was re-run against the true precondition, and it still failed - which no amount of further reproduction would ever have revealed, because the reproduction kept working perfectly.
recommendation: 1. Before recording a mechanism, list everything your setup step changed - not everything you INTENDED it to change. Creating a file, pulling an image, running a build and starting a daemon all have side effects that are part of your experiment whether or not you named them. 2. Isolate: vary ONE thing and predict the result before running it. Two conditions that always travel together are one condition until you separate them (`LL-009`'s independence test, applied to preconditions rather than to instruments). 3. Treat the FIX as the real experiment - apply it against the true failing precondition and require the symptom to disappear. A fix that fails there falsifies the mechanism, and that is the cheapest falsification available. 4. When a measurement is used to RULE OUT a rival explanation, record the ambient state it was taken in; a number that eliminates a hypothesis deserves more scrutiny than one that supports it, because eliminating closes off the search.
rationale: A reproduction is an existence proof over a conjunction: it shows that the set of things you changed is jointly sufficient. Attributing the effect to one member of that set is an inference the reproduction does not license, and nothing about the experience of watching the failure return distinguishes the two. The feeling of rigour scales with how reliably the symptom returns, which is exactly the wrong signal - a confounded setup reproduces just as reliably as an isolated one, often more so, because it changes more.
impact_if_followed: A recorded mechanism is one that survived an attempt to separate it from its neighbours, so the fix built on it works the first time and the register stops carrying confident causes that were never isolated.
impact_if_ignored: A wrong cause ships with the full rhetoric of proof - 'reproduced', 'measured', 'discarded' - into rows, prompts, memory and commit messages that cannot be amended, and the fix built on it fails while the diagnosis it rests on keeps being cited.

title: A defence-in-depth layer can be structurally invisible to every test that enters through the front door
statement: A DEFENCE-IN-DEPTH LAYER CAN BE STRUCTURALLY INVISIBLE TO EVERY TEST THAT ENTERS THROUGH THE FRONT DOOR, AND THE MORE LAYERS YOU ADD THE MORE OF THEM BECOME UNTESTABLE THAT WAY. A layer's correctness is only observable through a request that REACHES it, so whenever an EARLIER layer refuses the entire population that a LATER layer exists to refuse, the later layer's rule cannot be exercised from outside at all. That is not a gap in the tests; it is a property of the composition, and it gets WORSE as protection improves, because each new outer layer shadows more of the inner ones. The shadowed layers are exactly the ones a future refactor can weaken with no test noticing.
context: WBS-24.8 guards a targeting parameter with three independent layers: an SPA route guard, a path gate that refuses guest-only principals, and a role set on the query itself. The source asserted that adding Guest to that role set was 'the single mutation' that would let a guest read somebody else's slot. Written rather than measured, and FALSE: the path gate intercepts every guest before any handler runs, so the mutation can be applied and ALL TEN of the surface's HTTP tests stay green. Demonstrated by applying it rather than by argument.
recommendation: Two parts. FIRST, for each layer ask which population it UNIQUELY refuses; where the answer is 'none, from outside', assert that layer at its own boundary instead - here, against the authorization pipeline directly, with no HTTP and no middleware. SECOND, give each layer a DISTINGUISHABLE SIGNATURE and assert on the signature rather than on the status code: a path gate that sets a refusal-reason header and an application-layer refusal that emits an audit row can be told apart, whereas three tests all asserting 403 read as rigour while testing whichever layer happens to run first, and would keep passing if any one of them were deleted. And treat every 'the single X', 'the only way' or 'cannot' written about a control as a request to run the mutation - that is LL-028 applied to a security claim rather than a measurement.
impact_if_followed: Each layer is proven independently and by its own evidence, so the composition can be rearranged later without silently losing a control; and the false-confidence sentence gets caught while it is still a draft.
impact_if_ignored: A weakened inner layer ships silently. The tests that appear to cover it are covering an outer layer, so removing or narrowing the inner rule changes nothing visible until the outer layer is itself moved or relaxed - at which point the exposure is immediate and nothing in the suite ever flagged it.

title: A refactor can push a file under a per-file coverage floor without adding one untested line
statement: A REFACTOR CAN PUSH A FILE UNDER A PER-FILE COVERAGE FLOOR WITHOUT INTRODUCING A SINGLE NEW UNTESTED LINE, BECAUSE THE FLOOR IS A RATIO AND A REFACTOR MOVES THE DENOMINATOR. The inverse is equally invisible and matters more: ADDING covered code to a file raises its percentage and can carry pre-existing untested lines back over the threshold, so a file can silently STOP reporting a real gap because unrelated well-tested code landed beside it. A per-file ratio does not measure what is untested; it measures what is untested RELATIVE TO what is tested in the same file, and both halves move for reasons that have nothing to do with either.
context: Extracting a shared composer moved about thirty-six lines of COVERED composition out of one handler, taking it from 191 source lines to roughly 155. Three early-return guards in that file had never been executed by any test and still were not; nothing about them changed. Their share of a smaller file crossed the five per cent budget and CI failed the file - which reads unambiguously as 'the code you just added is untested' and sends the next reader to inspect new code they will find fully covered.
recommendation: When a per-file floor fails after a refactor, diff the UNCOVERED LINE NUMBERS against the previous run before diagnosing anything - not the percentage, and not the file. If the set is unchanged, the refactor EXPOSED a pre-existing gap rather than creating one, and the record should say so. The gap is still worth closing; what is wrong is the story about where it came from.
impact_if_followed: The diagnosis matches the cause, the commit message and the verdict attribute the gap honestly, and the pre-existing guards get forced instead of being carried further.
impact_if_ignored: Two failures. Time is spent auditing correctly-covered new code while the real gap sits in untouched guards; and in the opposite direction a genuine gap disappears from the report when unrelated covered code is added, so the floor stops reporting something it never stopped being true about.

title: A test whose fixture is the LIVE register is a test whose meaning changes when somebody does ordinary work - and the dangerous outcome is not the failure, it is the pass
statement: A TEST WHOSE FIXTURE IS THE LIVE REGISTER IS A TEST WHOSE MEANING CHANGES WHEN SOMEBODY DOES ORDINARY WORK, AND THE DANGEROUS OUTCOME IS NOT THE FAILURE - IT IS THE PASS. If a test SELECTS its subject from mutable state rather than constructing it, then a promotion, a status flip or an added row can silently substitute a different subject; the mutation still applies, the code still runs, and the assertion is now about something that was never under test. It may still pass - for a reason that has nothing to do with what the test names.
context: A three-case regression suite was written for the slice-review slate generator (DEF-117, DEF-119) and committed. Its third case was a deliberate calibration: strip the recorded reason out of a criterion-less work item and assert the generator STILL refuses it. Each case copied the store to a scratch tree and set ONE row's lifecycle_status to Review, leaving every sibling as the live register happened to have it. Hours later, in the same session, the operator promoted that row to Implemented (DEC-092). The calibration's mutation still applied and the generator still ran - but on a DIFFERENT item, never under test, which carried a citation and therefore rendered. Filed as DEF-120.
recommendation: Stage the whole SELECTION, never one row. Force the row under test into the state that selects it, force every sibling OUT of that state, and write the shape being tested into the row rather than inheriting it - so the case asserts a PROPERTY of the code under test rather than a fact about today's register. Then demand the cheap proof that the coupling is gone: the fixed test must pass under the exact live state that broke it. THE DISCRIMINATOR FOR SPOTTING IT BEFORE IT BITES: ask what a normal day's work would have to change for this test to stop testing what it names. If the answer is a status column, an added row, or a promotion - anything a colleague could do without touching the code under test - the fixture is coupled and the pass is not load-bearing.
rationale: THE LOUD FAILURE WAS LUCK, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE LESSON. The surviving Review row happened to carry a DW- citation, so the generator exited 0 against an expected 2 and the breakage was visible. Had that row instead lacked citations - one title-edit away, and the ordinary state of an item early in its life - the generator would have exited 2 WITH THE EXPECTED MESSAGE FOR A COMPLETELY DIFFERENT REASON, and the calibration would have reported PASS while testing nothing, indefinitely. A calibration that can pass for the wrong reason is the hollow pass it exists to prevent. IT IS NOT SIMPLY 'MOCK YOUR DATA': reading real rows was the right call and is what makes the suite meaningful, since it exercises real shapes a fixture would not. The error was finer - the SUBJECT SELECTION came from live mutable state rather than being established by the test. The generator's input is 'the set of rows at Review in slice X', so a test of it must CONSTRUCT that set.
impact_if_followed: Regression suites over the Tamheed package keep meaning what they say as rows are promoted, added and re-statused in the ordinary course of work, and a calibration that stops discriminating fails loudly instead of going quietly green.
impact_if_ignored: A hollow pass in the regression suite for the instrument that discharges LL-011, which would eventually let an unrenderable work item reach an operator review as a hand-built page - the exact harm DEF-116 and DEF-117 were filed to prevent. More generally it is LL-015's fault (a true result about the wrong set) operating on a test fixture instead of on a scan scope, and LL-013's fault-injection cannot catch it, because the injection lands on a subject the test no longer examines.

title: A control term proves the scan reached the corpus - it cannot prove your pattern matches the corpus's SPELLING of the thing you are looking for, and a hyphen is enough to return a confident zero
statement: A CONTROL TERM PROVES THE SCAN REACHED THE CORPUS. IT CANNOT PROVE THAT YOUR PATTERN MATCHES THE CORPUS'S SPELLING OF THE CONCEPT YOU ARE ACTUALLY LOOKING FOR - BECAUSE THE CONTROL IS A DIFFERENT TOKEN, AND ITS ORTHOGRAPHY IS NOT THE ONE UNDER TEST. A multi-word concept can be spelled with hyphens, spaces, camelCase or an abbreviation, and a pattern that picks one of those returns ZERO over a register that consistently uses another. The zero looks exactly like an absence, the control passes honestly, and every discipline in the checklist has been followed.
context:
DW-093 was filed with a measured claim: a sweep of six registers for `SoD-4` OR THE COI RULE returns ZERO rows, against a control term `SoD` non-zero in five of six - so 'nothing in the live package knows this control is unbuilt'. The row was activated on that basis (DEC-094 d1) and scheduled as WBS-26.1.

The pre-interview sweep for that item re-ran the question with wider keys and returned THREE rows the original had not: FR-076 (a requirement that specifies the conflict-of-interest feature and specifies its strength SOFTLY - the declaration is recorded WITHOUT automatic exclusion), DW-004 (Phase 2) and ADR-0010. Those three changed the interview: without them WBS-26.1 would have been built with a COI exclusion that FR-076's own words forbid, pulling Phase-2 scope into v1.

THE CAUSE WAS ISOLATED RATHER THAN INFERRED, AND THE INSTRUMENT HAD BEEN RECORDED ALL ALONG - in the row's own custom_attributes: the pattern was `SoD-4|conflict of interest|COI exclusion`. The register spells it `conflict-of-interest`, with hyphens. Measured with ONE variable changed and nothing else, over the same six registers: `conflict of interest` returns 1 row, `conflict-of-interest` returns 7, and the delta is exactly the three missed rows plus this row's own descendants.

TWO DETAILS SHARPEN IT. First, the ONE row the original pattern did match was DW-093 ITSELF - the sweep found its own query string and nothing else, which is trap 30's 'a scanner you write can measure itself'. Second, and worse: the LL-013 control discipline WAS followed. `SoD` was run, it was non-zero in five of six registers, and it was honest. But `SoD` is a different token, spelled identically everywhere, so it could only ever prove the scan reached the corpus. The half of the pattern that failed was never controlled at all.

A SECOND, SMALLER INSTANCE FIRED IN THE SAME HOUR, ON ME. I reported to the operator - and wrote into DEC-095's rationale - that the original sweep's instrument 'was never recorded, so any account of the cause would be a guess'. It WAS recorded, in custom_attributes, which I had not read because I had read the row's title. LL-006's 'read the thing itself' firing on the very row I was correcting.
recommendation: For every MULTI-WORD concept in a sweep pattern, allow the separators the corpus might use (`conflict[- ]of[- ]interest`) rather than picking one. Choose at least one control term that is SPELLED THE SAME WAY as the term under test, not merely a term you expect to be present - a control made of a different token can only prove the scan reached the corpus. Better still, before trusting a zero, grep the corpus for the concept's bare head-word (`conflict`) and READ what spelling comes back: the corpus's own orthography is cheaper to observe than to predict. And RECORD THE PATTERN beside the result, as DW-093 did - that is the only reason this was diagnosable at all rather than a permanent 'unknown'.
rationale: Sharpens LL-013 (a control proves the scanner had a subject) and LL-015 (a scan's SCOPE is part of its answer) by naming a case where BOTH disciplines were followed and the zero was still wrong - the gap is not scope and not subject, it is ORTHOGRAPHY. Trap 30 (a scanner you write can measure itself) is the shape of the self-match.
impact_if_followed: A register sweep's zero becomes trustworthy for the reason it claims to be. The three rows that changed DEC-095's second ruling would have surfaced when DW-093 was first filed, before the row was activated and scheduled.
impact_if_ignored: A silent false absence in the instrument LL-005, LL-008 and trap 32 all mandate before disposing of a capability or putting an option to the operator. It survives the LL-013 control discipline intact, and its output is a zero that reads as a finding. Here it would have built a COI exclusion into WBS-26.1 that FR-076's own words forbid, pulling Phase-2 scope into v1 without a scope change.

Delta = FR-076, DW-004, ADR-0010 (+ descendants of DW-093)."}

title: A sizing read off a class's own declaration misses what its BASE class already provides - and an unused parameter in the derived signature reads as evidence that it does not
statement: WHEN YOU SIZE WORK BY READING A CLASS, YOU ARE READING ITS OWN DECLARATION - AND WHATEVER ITS BASE CLASS ALREADY PROVIDES IS INVISIBLE IN EXACTLY THE PLACE YOU ARE LOOKING. The failure is not carelessness about the file; it is that the file is the wrong unit. It gets worse when the derived type carries a parameter or field that LOOKS like the missing thing: an unused parameter reads as evidence that the capability is absent, because if it were present the parameter would presumably be doing something.
context:
Sizing WBS-26.1 (SoD-4), I recorded three structural gaps into the plan row, DEC-096's rationale and SC-040: the recorder is not persisted, the topic owner is not exposed, the presenter is not exposed. TWO WERE RIGHT. The first was wrong.

I read Decision.cs, saw that Decision.Draft takes `actorSub` and never stores it, and concluded the recorder was not persisted and would need a new field plus an EF migration. Both halves of that reasoning felt sound and one was load-bearing: the unused parameter looked like a stub for the very thing I was looking for.

Measured while building: Decision derives from AuditableEntity, which carries CreatedBy, and ModuleDbContext.StampAudit fills it from ICurrentUser for every entry in state Added. So Decision.CreatedBy IS the recorder's Keycloak subject and always has been. The proof was already in the repository twice over - SoD-2 keys off minutes.CreatedBy for exactly this purpose, and Governance's AuthorApprovedSelf keys off Invariant.CreatedBy - and a test asserts edge.CreatedBy equals the acting subject.

A migration WAS still needed, for the new conflict FLAG. That is what made the wrong claim survivable and is also why it is worth recording: the conclusion (write a migration) came out right, so nothing downstream failed, and the reason was wrong the whole time.
recommendation: When sizing whether a field exists on an entity, read its BASE TYPES before its own declaration, not after - the base is where cross-cutting stamps, audit fields, concurrency tokens and soft-delete markers live, and it is the half a reader of one file never sees. Then look for a SIBLING that already solves the same problem: two existed here and either would have answered it in seconds. And treat an unused parameter as a QUESTION rather than as evidence - it is as likely to be dead as to be a stub, and which one it is decides the estimate.
rationale: It is LL-006's family (read the thing itself, not a proxy) with a specific and repeatable mechanism: the proxy was the derived class's own source, which is normally the RIGHT thing to read. It also pairs with the trap that a corrected measurement does not correct the inference built on it - here the inference (a migration is needed) happened to survive its own false premise, which is exactly the case where nothing forces the correction.
impact_if_followed: A sizing that names structural gaps names the ones that exist. In this instance one of three claimed gaps evaporated, and the two siblings that disproved it were both already in the codebase.
impact_if_ignored: A plan row, a decision's rationale and a scope change all carry a false structural claim, and the operator rules on scope with it in front of them. Here the ruling was not changed by it, which is luck rather than process - a false constraint on a decision slate is read at the moment of deciding by the one person who cannot check it.

Two in-repo siblings already key off it: MinutesOfMeeting.CreatedBy for SoD-2, Invariant.CreatedBy for Governance's AuthorApprovedSelf.", "survivable_because": "a migration was needed anyway, for the new flag - so the conclusion was right while its stated reason was false"}

title: A remedy that reduces a PROBABILITY cannot be falsified by the failure recurring - the recurrence gets attributed to the residual it openly admits
statement: WHEN A FIX REDUCES THE LIKELIHOOD OF A FAILURE RATHER THAN REMOVING ITS CONDITION, IT BUYS AN UNFALSIFIABLE POSITION, AND THE HONESTY OF ITS OWN CAVEAT IS WHAT MAKES IT UNFALSIFIABLE. State the residual - *it removes the dominant cause, not every case* - and every later recurrence has a ready explanation that is not *the fix was wrong*. The register then accumulates a remedy nothing can ever retire, on a row that reads as diligent because it disclosed its own limits. **Prefer a remedy that changes the CONDITION over one that changes the ODDS, and when only the odds are reachable, say so as a deferral rather than as a fix.**
context: DEF-122: a rate-limit test asserted a property of a 60-second fixed window using three sequential HTTP requests whose spacing nothing bounded. The agent recommended warming the host outside the limiter's partition so the first request's cold-start cost fell outside the window, and wrote the residual into the recommendation itself - *it removes the DOMINANT cost, not every possible slow request*. The operator refused the fix and required the mechanism to be isolated first (DEC-101 d1). The isolation then showed the failure condition is ANY gap larger than the window between the first permit acquisition and the last request, so a slow second request, a GC pause or thread-pool starvation mid-sequence produces the identical failure - and the warm-up addresses none of them. The shipped fix instead issues the requests CONCURRENTLY, so every permit is taken within microseconds and the window cannot roll mid-sequence at all.
recommendation: Before proposing a fix, ask what OBSERVATION would prove it wrong. If the answer is *none - a recurrence would just mean the residual fired*, it is a mitigation and must be labelled one. Then look for the remedy that removes the condition instead: here, three requests whose ORDER in time is unconstrained became three requests issued TOGETHER, which is not a smaller window of risk but no window at all. When the condition genuinely cannot be removed, file the mitigation with an explicit statement that it is one, so a later recurrence is read as the known gap rather than as a new mystery.
rationale: It is LL-029's neighbour and not a duplicate. LL-029 governs DIAGNOSIS - a reproduction proves sufficiency, never causation. This governs the REMEDY that follows one, and it bites even when the diagnosis is right: a correct-but-partial cause invites a fix sized to the part you saw. The two failed together here, which is what makes the pair worth separating: the mechanism was un-isolated AND the proposed fix was probabilistic, and each would have hidden the other. It is also the THIRTY-FIFTH's shape moved one step earlier in time - there a confounded setup reproduced MORE reliably because it changed more, and only the fix FAILING caught it; here the fix could never have failed legibly, so nothing would have caught it at all.
impact_if_followed: A remedy either removes a failure condition or is recorded as a deferral with a named residual. Either way a later recurrence is informative: it either falsifies the fix or confirms the known gap.
impact_if_ignored: The register fills with fixes that cannot be retired and cannot be disproved. Each recurrence is absorbed by the caveat, the row stays Fixed, and the underlying condition is never removed - while the disclosure of the residual makes the whole thing read as rigour.

Identical wall clock between the latter two, opposite outcomes, so 'the test was slow' is eliminated.", "shipped_fix": "Issue the requests concurrently and assert the COUNT of throttled responses, not which one. PR #332 -> 4529fd01.", "relation_to_LL_029": "LL-029 is about diagnosis (reproduction proves sufficiency, not causation). This is about the remedy that follows a diagnosis, and it bites even when the diagnosis is correct but partial."}

title: A PR-head run and a merge-commit run are DIFFERENT runs over identical code, and `gh pr checks` only ever shows you the first
statement: AFTER A SQUASH-MERGE, THE TREE THAT LANDS ON THE TARGET BRANCH GETS ITS OWN CI RUN, AND IT CAN DISAGREE WITH THE RUN THAT GATED THE PR EVEN THOUGH `git diff` BETWEEN THE TWO IS EMPTY. On this repository the two have now disagreed twice. **So *CI was green* is not a fact until you say WHICH RUN.** Cite the run id: a run id cannot be attributed to the wrong tree, while a colour can. And a merge is a push to the target branch, so the obligation to poll that branch's CI to completion applies to it exactly as it does to a direct commit.
context: Two failures in one session. (1) AV-235's evidence field asserted *'CI on the merged tree: frontend, backend and compose all success, plus E2E and Security'*. Measured: the merge commit c273294c's CI run 33297623382 concluded FAILURE with the backend job red, and E2E does not run on `push` at all so no E2E result for that tree exists. The green being described was PR #331's head 6e8d4b96, whose three runs finished at 06:43:15Z - two minutes before the merge run started. Corrected by appending AV-236. (2) The same conflation reached the kickoff prompt, which recorded #331 as merging *'with ten checks green'*, and the red then sat unrecorded on main for a whole session until the next session's orientation block ran `gh run list`.
recommendation: Write the run id into any claim about CI, never a colour alone - `run 33297623382 (push, main) => failure` rather than *the merge was green*. After a merge, poll the TARGET BRANCH's run to completion before recording anything that depends on it; `gh pr checks` answers a different question and will happily report all-green while the branch is red. When a defect or verdict cites CI, the citation is the run id and the event type, because the event type is what tells you which tree was tested.
rationale: The mechanism is that the two runs are triggered by different events over trees that are byte-identical in `src/` and `tests/`, so every instinct that says *the code is the same, the result is the same* is wrong for reasons that have nothing to do with the code. Worse, the failure is INVISIBLE to every gate: a verdict's evidence is free text and nothing in the store compares an evidence claim to the run it names, so G-PROGRESS, acs-met and the prose-status checker all pass over it. The only thing that catches it is quoting an id somebody can resolve.
impact_if_followed: A CI claim can be checked by anyone later, because it names a resolvable artifact. A red on the target branch is found in minutes rather than a session later.
impact_if_ignored: Verdicts carry evidence that is confidently wrong about which tree was tested, and a red branch is recorded as green in a defect row, a prompt and a memory index at once - none of which disagree with each other, because they all came from one misreading.
