title: A re-run is not a second sample of the question you are asking - it is a fresh sample of every OTHER question the suite asks
statement: WHEN YOU ARGUE THAT RE-RUNNING A SUITE CAN TEACH YOU NOTHING BECAUSE YOU ALREADY HOLD THE ANSWER TO THE QUESTION IT WAS RUN FOR, YOU ARE TREATING A WHOLE TEST SUITE AS A ONE-BIT INSTRUMENT. It re-asks every assertion it contains. A suite of hundreds of tests re-run on unchanged code is a fresh draw on all of them, and a latent, timing-dependent or environment-dependent defect that has passed hundreds of times can surface on any draw. **The cost of a re-run is bounded and known; the value is not bounded by the question that prompted it.**
context: DEC-100 d2. main was red on a container-startup failure and the operator ruled the failed backend job be re-run to restore a green. The agent recommended against, on the reasoning that a green already existed on byte-identical code (the PR head), so the re-run could produce no fact the register did not already hold - an argument about the ONE question, container startup, which was sound about that question. The re-run failed on a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT test: a rate-limit test whose timing assumption had presumably held for hundreds of runs, filed as DEF-122 and since fixed. The container test passed on that draw, so the agent's own question came back green and the answer to it was indeed uninformative - which is exactly why the argument felt right and was still wrong.
recommendation: Cost a re-run against what the whole suite could surface, not against the question that prompted it. When arguing that an action is uninformative, name the specific claim it cannot inform and check whether the action does anything ELSE - a re-run executes every assertion, a rebuild exercises every layer, a redeploy touches every service. Reserve *this can teach us nothing* for instruments that genuinely answer one question.
rationale: The error is a scope slip in the agent's own reasoning: *this cannot answer X* was written as *this cannot produce a fact*. It is LL-015's family - an instrument's output measures the set it actually ran over, not the set you had in mind - applied to the value of running an instrument at all rather than to reading its result. It also stands as a recorded case where an operator override produced a finding the agent's reasoning would have foreclosed, which is worth keeping precisely because the reasoning-against is preserved in DEC-100 d2 and must not be read later as having been sound.
impact_if_followed: Cheap, bounded re-executions are costed honestly, and latent defects that only a fresh draw can surface get their chance to appear before a user finds them.
impact_if_ignored: An agent talks an operator out of a bounded action by a locally valid argument about one question, and the defects the action would have surfaced stay latent until they fire somewhere more expensive.

title: A lifecycle status can be LOAD-BEARING rather than lagging, and the reason may live only in a progress entry no register view surfaces
statement: BEFORE 'REPAIRING' A ROW WHOSE STATUS LOOKS BEHIND ITS EVIDENCE, ASK WHETHER THE STATUS IS DOING WORK. A store constraint keyed on status - here, immutability that fires on `Approved` and not on `Proposed` - makes the un-promoted state the ENABLER of something, and promoting it is then not a tidy-up but a demolition. **The tell is UNIFORMITY: six of six rows in one slice is a decision; two of six is an oversight.** And the reason will not be in any register view - not in a status query, not in a readiness rule, not in a gate - because the thing that records a deliberate exploitation of a constraint is prose. **Sweep progress entries, not only decisions and ADRs: a progress entry is a ruling's record too.**
context: AC-088..AC-093 sat at `Proposed` with `Met` latest verdicts while 135 of 157 acceptance criteria were `Approved`, in a slice (SL-028) that was itself `Implemented`. The agent measured the shape, checked LL-006's trap by asking whether any DECISION or ADR had ever named the rows - three of the six were named by none - and concluded 'not previously ruled'. The operator ruled investigate-before-touching. PE-375 then gave the cause in terms: SL-028 was created RETROACTIVELY because FR-156 carried no implements edge, and the six criteria 'were bound to it directly - free, because the immutability trigger does not fire on Proposed'. Their un-promoted status is what made the binding possible. Promoting them would have made six deliberately-mutable criteria immutable, one-way, and would have destroyed the property the binding programme depended on.
recommendation: When a status looks stale against its evidence, run three checks before touching it. (1) Is it UNIFORM across a natural group? Uniformity is the signature of a decision. (2) Does any store constraint key on that status - immutability, a CHECK, a trigger, a foreign-key rule? If so the status may be load-bearing. (3) Sweep PROGRESS ENTRIES for the row's identifier, not just decisions and ADRs - LL-006's 'read the thing itself' extends to reading the thing that explains it, and that is often prose in an append-only log. Only then decide, and weight the decision by reversibility: an irreversible promotion made on an unmeasured cause cannot be undone.
rationale: It is LL-006's family - read the thing itself, not a proxy - with two additions that are not in LL-006. First, the thing to read may not be the ROW: every register view agreed with itself here and all of them were silent on the reason. Second, it supplies a positive TELL rather than only a warning: uniformity across a group distinguishes a decision from an oversight cheaply, before any deeper reading. It is also the reversibility half of DEC-101 d1's standard - that ruling said isolate a mechanism before writing a fix; this says the bar rises further when the action cannot be undone.
impact_if_followed: A status that is doing work is left alone, and a status that is merely lagging is corrected on a known cause. Irreversible edits are made only when the reason for the current state is established.
impact_if_ignored: A tidy-up destroys a deliberate state whose reason was recorded somewhere nothing queries, and where the edit is one-way there is no recovery - the register looks more consistent and has lost a property something depended on.

title: A GitHub Actions job reported `skipped` conflates two unrelated causes - the `if:` was false, and a job in `needs:` did not succeed - and the API prints the same word for both
statement: `skipped` IS NOT A REASON, IT IS AN OUTCOME WITH AT LEAST TWO CAUSES, AND THE ONE YOU CAN SEE IN THE WORKFLOW FILE IS THE ONE YOU WILL PICK. A job with both an `if:` condition and a `needs:` list reports `skipped` when the condition evaluates false AND when any needed job did not succeed. Reading the `if:` expression, seeing `skipped`, and concluding the condition was false is a match that fits and is not evidence. **The discriminator costs one query: read the conclusions of the jobs it NEEDS, or find a run where they passed.** More generally: when a status has several possible causes and only one of them is visible in the artifact you happen to be reading, you have not measured the cause - you have matched it.
context: Sizing WBS-26.3 I recorded that ci.yml's publish job 'is gated on github.event_name == push && github.ref == refs/heads/main && vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN != \'\', and it reported skipped on the #331 merge run, SO THE VARIABLE IS UNSET.' The observation was true; the cause was invented. Measured later, with a control: gh variable list returns AWS_ROLE_ARN set on 2026-08-04, three weeks earlier, and publish has needs: [backend, frontend, compose]. On the run in question backend FAILED, so publish was a dependency casualty. On the very next main run backend succeeded and publish=success. The if: gate had been satisfiable throughout. The needs: line sat ONE LINE ABOVE the if: in the same file and I did not read it.
recommendation: Never report why a job was skipped from the workflow file alone. Check both causes: (1) the conclusions of every job in its `needs:` on that same run, and (2) whether the `if:` expression's inputs are actually unset - for repository variables that is `gh variable list`, which is one command. Best of all, find a CONTROL run where the needed jobs passed: if the job ran there, the `if:` was never the blocker. And when writing the finding down, record what you MEASURED (`publish reported skipped on run N`) separately from what you INFERRED (`therefore the variable is unset`), so a later reader can see which half to distrust.
rationale: It is LL-020's family - a conclusion built on a misread does not travel with the correction - caught one step earlier, at the moment the conclusion is formed rather than after it has propagated. It is also LL-006's 'read the thing itself' with a specific target: the thing to read was the `needs:` line, not the `if:` line, and both were in the same file within one line of each other. No gate can see this class: every identifier resolves, every status is correct, and the false half is a CAUSE attached to a true observation.
impact_if_followed: A claim about why CI did something is either measured or is labelled an inference, and the cheap discriminator - a control run, or one variable query - is run before the claim is written down.
impact_if_ignored: An invented cause propagates into plan rows, decision text, progress entries and commit messages, and commit messages cannot be amended. Here it reached four artifacts plus a PR body before a colour change in an unrelated run exposed it.

title: A CLOSED row is an unindexed decision store: operator decisions get recorded inside Fixed defects, where no decision-register sweep can ever find them
statement: WHEN YOU SWEEP FOR *WHAT WAS DECIDED*, YOU SWEEP DECISIONS, ADRs AND OPEN QUESTIONS - AND A REAL DECISION MAY BE SITTING IN A `Fixed` DEFECT ROW, WHICH READS AS A CLOSED PROBLEM RATHER THAN AS A RULING. Measured in this package: **10 of 113 closed defect rows record an operator decision**, including one - `DEF-079` - that a later work item was scoped to REVERSE without anyone noticing, because every sweep for a governing decision came back empty. **A row's lifecycle status tells you the problem is closed; it tells you nothing about whether the row also holds a ruling that still binds.** And the same rows' PROSE is not maintained after closure: a status is corrected when the work lands, the surrounding sentences usually are not.
context: WBS-26.4 was scoped to switch compose dependents from service_started to service_healthy, on DW-091's claim that a misleading comment had concealed an oversight. The pre-build sweep found the opposite: service_healthy had been declared, its total-outage consequence measured, put back to the operator, and reversed by their choice - all recorded in DEF-079, a Fixed defect row. Sweeping decisions, ADRs and open questions for the trade returned nothing. Generalising the class then found that 10 of 113 closed defect rows carry operator decisions, and that two of them (DEF-094, DEF-031) carry PROSE that is now false while their statuses are correct: DEF-094 still offers disposition options for a disposition long taken and says no AC exists when AC-122 is Approved and Met; DEF-031's open_gap says backup failures have no alerting path when backup.sh publishes to SNS from an EXIT trap.
recommendation: Add closed rows to the *what was decided* sweep, not only open ones - `Fixed`, `Won't-fix` and `Obsolete` defects, and closed deferred-work rows. Grep them for decision language (*put back to the operator*, *the operator chose*, *operator decision*) as well as for the identifier you care about. ⚠ **Read the hits rather than counting them: tense is invisible to a regex.** *"Needed an operator decision"* followed by *"✅ DECIDED"* is history, not an open question - two of the ten flagged that way and both were clean. And when a row's status changes, **re-read its prose in the same batch**: a status is one column and the sentences around it are another, and nothing in the store compares them.
rationale: It is LL-038's family - a state can be load-bearing and its reason may live where no register view looks - with the specific, checkable location this package keeps using. LL-038's instances have now been a progress entry, no record at all, a code comment, a closed defect row, and stale prose inside a correctly-statused row; this names the fourth and fifth and gives them a sweep. It also inherits LL-006's rule (read the thing itself) with a warning attached: the sweep that finds these rows CANNOT adjudicate them, because the discriminator between a live question and a narrated one is grammatical.
impact_if_followed: A work item is never scoped to reverse a decision nobody could find, and a closed row's prose is corrected when its status is. The sweep for governing decisions covers where decisions actually are, rather than where the schema suggests they should be.
impact_if_ignored: An item gets activated, decided and scheduled on a premise a closed row already refuted - which is exactly what happened to WBS-26.4, costing a scope change and a blocked build - and closed rows accumulate prose that reads as open work, inviting sessions to re-do settled things or to re-litigate settled ones.

title: Proving a scanner RAN is not proving it had a SUBJECT. A test-count delta is evidence about the spec, never about the assertion.
statement: WHEN YOU SHOW THAT A CHECK EXECUTED, YOU HAVE ANSWERED A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM THE ONE THAT MATTERS. `LL-013` says prove the scanner looked at something by injecting a fault and watching the count move. THE GAP IS THAT THE COUNT CAN MOVE FOR THE SPEC WHILE THE ASSERTION INSIDE IT LOOKS AT NOTHING. `WBS-24.2` added an axe sweep for the backlog calendar and proved it ran rather than inferring it from a green job - the e2e test count moved 86 to 88, which is a real measurement and was correctly presented as one. **It was sound and insufficient.** The seed put every meeting one day outside the month the calendar renders, so for weeks `expect(axeViolations(page)).toEqual([])` asserted over a grid with no chips in it, and the chips were the only thing on that view capable of violating anything. The sweep reported clean the entire time and the violation was `serious`.
context: DEF-126, 2026-09-01. scenario.ts pinned every seeded meeting to the fixed date 2026-09-01 and both calendars open on the current month, so the assertion had no subject until the clock reached that date - at which point a PR that changed only a C# storage adapter went red on an accessibility rule. The violation (.cal-event, a <button> about 21px tall against WCAG 2.2 target-size's 24x24) had existed since the sweep was written.
recommendation: For any assertion of an ABSENCE - no violations, no errors, no matches, no rows - assert the PRESENCE of the thing being examined first, in the same test. `await expect(page.locator('.cal-event').first()).toBeVisible()` before the axe call; a non-empty result set before a NotContain; a subject count printed by a scanner before it reports clean. And prefer a subject the test SEEDS ITSELF over one it inherits from whatever else has run: an inherited subject is an accident, and an accident can stop happening without anyone editing anything.
rationale: It is LL-013 with the hole closed. LL-013 asks for the instrument to be calibrated; this asks for the instrument to be shown POINTING AT SOMETHING at the moment it reports. The two come apart whenever the subject is data rather than code, because a fault injected into the CHECK proves the check works while saying nothing about whether today's data reaches it. This project has now filed the same shape four times as a green control that is blind (DEF-078, DEF-087, DEF-123, DEF-126); the first three were controls that could not see, and this one is a control that could see perfectly and had nothing in front of it.
impact_if_followed: An absence assertion becomes falsifiable. A sweep that stops having a subject fails loudly on the day it stops, rather than reporting clean until an unrelated change happens to restore the subject.
impact_if_ignored: A check accumulates credit it has not earned. The longer it passes, the more confidently it is cited - WBS-24.2's row cited its count delta as proof - and the discovery arrives as an unrelated PR going inexplicably red, which invites the conclusion that the PR is at fault.

title: After setting a scope-change to Merged, re-read every row its delta edges name. `Merged` is an assertion that the delta was applied, and nothing checks the assertion.
statement: A `scope-change` row carries `scope_adds`/`scope_modifies`/`scope_removes` edges naming the rows it changes, and the obligation is to apply those changes and THEN set the `SC-` to `Merged`. THE TWO HALVES ARE NOT COUPLED BY ANYTHING. The `scope-changes-merged` readiness rule selects `Approved` scope changes whose deltas never merged - so once an `SC-` says `Merged` the rule passes and NEVER LOOKS AT THE ROW THE DELTA NAMES. `SC-042` was approved, set `Merged`, and its `scope_modifies` target `WBS-26.4` was never updated: the item went on reading *BLOCKED ON A FRESH RULING AND NO CODE HAS BEEN WRITTEN* and *IF THIS ITEM IS REBUILT IN ANY FORM IT NEEDS A scope-change ROW FIRST* - a demand the `SC-` had already satisfied. `gate_run` was 7/7 throughout and every identifier resolved.
context: Found 2026-09-01 in the pre-interview sweep, a day after SC-042 was merged. A fresh session resolving the live slice and reading its open items would have found WBS-26.4 blocked pending a ruling that had already been given, and either stopped or re-run the interview. prm-next.md's own numbered list said 'the item's deliverable is now in its own row and in SC-042' - a promise the row was breaking.
recommendation: Treat `Merged` as the LAST step, not the first: apply the delta to every row the edges name, re-read those rows, and only then set the `SC-`. If the `SC-` is already `Merged`, run `trace_query` on it and open each target - the edges are the checklist. And when the target row's prose contains an instruction the scope change discharges (*this needs an SC- first*, *do not edit X*), that sentence is part of the delta and has to be rewritten with the rest.
rationale: It is the unrelated-columns failure this package keeps recording - a requirement's status versus its DW- row's, an AC's lifecycle_status versus its verdicts, a test row versus the file it names - arriving between a scope change and the row it modifies. LL-040 names the same shape for closed rows whose prose outlives their status. The common cause is that a status is one column and the sentences around it are another, and no gate in the store compares them.
impact_if_followed: A scope change either lands completely or is visibly unfinished. The row a delta names never contradicts the decision that changed it.
impact_if_ignored: A work item reads as blocked on a ruling that exists, or as unblocked when it is not, and the contradiction is invisible to every mechanical pass because the identifiers all resolve and the statuses are all correct.

title: A pattern that matches a DIFFERENT concept's spelling hands you a confident wrong subject, and that is harder to notice than a zero.
statement: `LL-033` warns that a control term proves the scan reached the corpus but not that your pattern matches the corpus's spelling of the concept you want. THE MIRROR IMAGE IS WORSE AND HAS NO CONTROL AT ALL: the pattern matches the corpus's spelling of SOMETHING ELSE, returns hits, and you reason about the wrong subject with no signal that anything went wrong. A grep for `cal-grid` matched `mt-cal-grid` as a SUBSTRING, listed the meetings calendar first, and a whole defect row was written about `.mt-cal-event` in `meetings.css` - quoting its CSS accurately, quoting the wrong file's design reference, and reaching a conclusion about an element the failing test never touches. **A zero would have prompted a second look. A hit did not.**
context: DEF-126's first version, 2026-09-01. The failing test asserts on page.locator('.cal-grid'), which is features/topics/Calendar.tsx; MeetingsCalendar renders .mt-cal-grid. The error was caught only by reading the component the row described in order to check a different question, and finding that its class name did not match the selector being reasoned about. The wrong component turned out to carry the same defect in a worse form, which is luck rather than method.
recommendation: When a search returns hits, confirm the hit IS the subject before reasoning from it - anchor the pattern (`"cal-grid"` with its delimiter, `^\.cal-event`, a word boundary) or open the file and check that the identifier appears in the form you meant. And when a finding names a file, read that file's own declaration of the thing you are describing: a component's class name, a method's signature, a rule's own text. It is DW-091's fault class in a different register - quoting a real artifact accurately and attributing it to the wrong place.
rationale: Substring matching is the default in every tool this project uses - grep without -w, Playwright's getByRole name matching, a plain `in` test in a script - and it fails silently in the direction that produces evidence rather than the direction that produces nothing. WBS-24.2 already recorded getByRole's substring behaviour matching 'Regular' and 'Extraordinary' for {name:'AR'}; this is the same mechanism applied to a file search, where the consequence is a wrong subject rather than a wrong element.
impact_if_followed: A finding names the artifact it is actually about. Corrections are to the analysis rather than to the record afterwards.
impact_if_ignored: A defect row, an operator decision and a fix can all be built on the wrong file while every quotation in them is accurate - and the accuracy of the quotations is what makes it convincing.

title: A hardcoded date in a fixture is a clock fixture: it makes a test mean something different every month, and it can go quiet again on its own.
statement: `LL-032` records that a test whose fixture is the LIVE REGISTER changes meaning when somebody does ordinary work, and that the dangerous outcome is the PASS. A FIXED DATE IS THE SAME FAULT WITH THE CLOCK AS THE MOVING PART, AND NOBODY HAS TO DO ANYTHING AT ALL. `scenario.ts` seeded every meeting at `2026-09-01T14:00:00.000Z` - called *"the original fixed future slot"* in its own comment, and genuinely future when it was written. Both calendars render the CURRENT month, so the seeded meeting was outside the view every month until September, present for one month, and outside it again from October. The assertion built on it was vacuous, then meaningful for thirty days, then vacuous again - **and only the middle state is visible as a failure.**
context: DEF-126, 2026-09-01. The literal was future when written, became the present, and would have become the past. A fixed date does not announce which of the three it is on any given run.
recommendation: In a fixture, express a date as a RELATION to now - the 15th of the current month, now plus seven days, the start of last quarter - and choose the offset so no boundary can be crossed by a timezone difference or a run that straddles midnight (the 15th, not the 1st or the 31st). Where a test needs a date in a particular relation to the clock (already ended, still upcoming), say so in the value rather than in a comment. ⚠ And check what else depends on the default before changing it: here, `GetMySession` filters `ScheduledEnd >= now` and would have been broken by a past-dated seed - except that it carries a documented fallback to the most recent meeting, which is why reading the implementation came before believing the alarm.
rationale: It extends LL-032 from a register to the clock, and adds the property that makes it worse: a register only changes when somebody works, so a broken fixture stays broken until someone acts, whereas a date fixture repairs and re-breaks itself on a calendar no one is watching. The self-healing is the dangerous half - a failure that stops occurring reads exactly like a failure that was fixed.
impact_if_followed: A fixture means the same thing on every run, and a test that depends on the clock says so in the value rather than by accident.
impact_if_ignored: An assertion silently changes what it is asserting about as time passes, fails on a date unrelated to any change, and then stops failing without anyone fixing anything - which is the strongest possible invitation to record it as a flake.

The 15th is chosen so no timezone offset and no run straddling midnight can push the meeting into an adjacent month.", "checked_before_changing": "GetMySession.cs filters ScheduledEnd >= now, which a past-dated seed would defeat - except it falls back to the most recent meeting. Read before believed; no other clock-dependent meeting filter exists in src."}

title: Text that has passed through a DISPLAY is unsafe to re-transmit, whatever its origin — and transcription fidelity is not a function of length, so length cannot be used to decide when to check.
statement:
TRAP 13 SAYS *build payloads from `data/*.jsonl`, never from `entity_query` output, because the store holds truncated rows* — and it names the STORE as the source of short text. THE TRUNCATION CAN JUST AS EASILY BE ON YOUR OWN SIDE OF THE PIPE. A field read from the canonical JSONL for the purpose of LOOKING at it, printed with a `[:400]` slice for readability, is exactly as dangerous as a truncated store read, and the guard *use the JSONL* does not fire on it because the JSONL genuinely was the source.

THE GENERAL FORM IS WIDER THAN THE TRAP AS WRITTEN: A FIELD IS SAFE TO RE-TRANSMIT ONLY IF IT CAME FROM A READ WHOSE PURPOSE WAS TRANSMISSION. Any text that has passed through a display — a terminal print, a summary line, a table, a preview, an excerpt — is suspect regardless of where it originally came from.

AND THE SECOND HALF IS WHAT MAKES A LENGTH HEURISTIC USELESS: TRANSCRIPTION FIDELITY DOES NOT DEGRADE WITH LENGTH IN THE WAY INTUITION PREDICTS. In one session a 9386-character field was re-transmitted byte-perfectly and a 2959-character field — shorter, and authored minutes earlier — came back with a silent word inserted. **So size cannot be used to decide which writes deserve a check. Every re-transmitted field gets the same hash-and-verify, or the practice is a coin flip dressed as a policy.**
context: 2026-09-01. Amending `DW-071` required a full row because `deferred_work.title` is NOT NULL. The payload's title was composed from a line of the session's OWN earlier sweep output, which had printed `title[:400]` for terminal readability. The upsert returned `ok` and destroyed 1697 of 2097 characters — every sentence after the first paragraph, including the whole coverage-gap argument and the row's explanation of why it was a deferred-work row rather than an acceptance criterion. In the same session, `SC-044`'s 2959-character description drifted by one inserted word while `WBS-26.4`'s 9386-character title, `DW-091`'s 6079 and `WBS-26.5`'s 6775 all went byte-perfect.
recommendation: Re-transmit a NOT NULL field only from a read taken FOR that transmission — emit it as a JSON literal from the canonical file and paste that, never a value that has been through a print, a summary or an excerpt. Hash the field BEFORE the write, compare after, and CALIBRATE the comparison by injecting a one-character corruption first (`LL-013`) — an equality check that has not been shown to discriminate proves nothing. Apply it to every field regardless of size, because size does not predict which one will drift. Where a row genuinely changed, prefer appending to it over re-typing it to preserve it, so the verification is a clean prefix check.
rationale: The failure is invisible to everything the package owns. `gate_run()` returns 7/7 over a 400-character title; `G-IDS` checks foreign keys and the entity index, not field lengths; `readiness_check` never reads the field; and no gate is column-level — the v2.3 migration already established that every gate is row-level, which is why it passed 7/7 while damaging register data. A truncated row simply stays truncated, and the loss is discoverable only by someone who happens to remember what used to be there. The pre-image that caught this existed only because hash-and-verify had been adopted earlier in the same session against a DIFFERENT hazard, so the catch was luck riding on an unrelated habit.
impact_if_followed: A silent field truncation becomes a loud, immediate failure with a byte-exact restore path, and the check is applied uniformly instead of by a size intuition that this instance disproved.
impact_if_ignored: Authoritative register rows lose most of their content on a write that reports success, with no gate, readiness rule or view able to report it — and the loss surfaces only if a human recalls the missing text.

title: A PRESCRIBED instrument can go stale against the artifact it measures, and it then returns a confident WRONG number rather than an error — so a documented command is a claim to re-verify, not an authority to quote.
statement:
`LL-033` warns that a pattern matching a spelling the corpus does not use hands back a confident wrong subject. THE SHARPER CASE IS WHEN THAT PATTERN IS THE ONE YOUR OWN DOCUMENTATION TELLS YOU TO RUN. A committed instruction to *measure it with this command* carries the authority of having been written deliberately, by someone who had checked — and it keeps that authority long after the artifact it measures has been rewritten underneath it.

THE FAILURE IS NOT THAT THE COMMAND ERRORS. It runs, it has a subject, it returns a plausible number, and the number is wrong. A prescribed grep for literal `page.goto('/x')` calls returned FIVE routes for an accessibility sweep that visits TWENTY-THREE, because the sweep had been rewritten to iterate a `ROUTES` array through a helper — a change that made the sweep four times wider and the prescribed instrument blind at the same moment.

**AN INSTRUMENT AND THE ARTIFACT IT MEASURES ARE ONE DECISION IN TWO PLACES, AND ONLY ONE OF THEM IS EXERCISED BY CI** — `LL-019`'s shape, moved from a pinned base image and its package repo onto a measurement and its subject. **What catches it is refusing a number that disagrees with something you independently know**, not re-reading the command.
context: 2026-09-01. `prm-next.md` carries the instruction *"DO NOT RE-QUOTE A COVERAGE RATIO FROM HERE; MEASURE IT"* followed by the exact command — a grep for `page.goto('…')` over `rtl-a11y.spec.ts`. Run as prescribed while measuring `DW-071`'s stale figure for an operator interview, it returned 5. PR `#336` had days earlier replaced the enumerated visits with a `SECRETARY_ROUTES` constant iterated by a `violationsByRoute` helper, adding 18 routes the literal pattern cannot see. The true figure is 23 distinct static routes. The wrong number was caught only because it contradicted a known event — `#336` was recorded as having swept 18 routes, which 5 cannot accommodate.
recommendation: Treat a documented measurement command as a claim with a date on it, not as an authority. Before quoting its output into anything durable, check it against something you know independently — a recorded event, a control term, a second key on a different property (`LL-009`: two instruments agreeing is one instrument when they share a mechanism). When an instrument and its subject can drift apart, say so where the instrument is written down, and prefer a pattern keyed on the artifact's STRUCTURE over one keyed on a spelling. Where a number will be put in front of the operator, state the instrument beside it so they can disagree with the instrument rather than with the figure (`PE-613`).
rationale: The prescription exists precisely because a stale COUNT was dangerous, so it was replaced with a command — the standing remedy of giving the command rather than the answer. But that remedy silently assumes the command is stable while only the answer moves. Here the command rotted and the answer it produced was worse than a stale figure would have been, because it arrived wearing the authority of a live measurement taken exactly as instructed. The instrument's own documentation cannot warn about this: it was correct when written, and nothing compares a documented pattern against the file it targets.
impact_if_followed: A documented measurement is re-verified against an independent fact before it enters a decision, so a rotted instrument is caught at the moment it would otherwise have been most persuasive.
impact_if_ignored: A wrong number reaches an operator interview or a durable record carrying the authority of the project's own prescribed method, and the disclaimer *measure it, do not quote it* actively vouches for it.

title: Choose the instrument by asking what a NEGATIVE result would mean — an instrument that cannot distinguish 'the hypothesis is wrong' from 'I cannot see it' turns every refutation into a coin flip you will read as a refutation.
statement: `LL-013` says prove the scanner looked at something before trusting a clean scan. THE PRIOR QUESTION IS WHETHER THE INSTRUMENT COULD HAVE PRODUCED A MEANINGFUL NEGATIVE AT ALL. `PE-769` measured a suspected memory leak by sampling the process WORKING SET on a 64 GB developer machine. On a box that never pressures the GC, working set is equally consistent with a leak and with ordinary lazy collection — so the baseline curve proved nothing, and, far worse, the intervention's UNCHANGED curve was equally consistent with 'the stores are not the cause' and with 'this instrument cannot see the difference'. The register was one step from carrying a confident REFUTED that the instrument had no power to support. The fix is one line — force a full collection and read retained MANAGED bytes (`GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); GC.Collect(); GC.GetTotalMemory(true)`), keeping working set as a secondary column — and with it the same experiment refuted the store hypothesis at 345 MB vs 335 MB and confirmed the real one at 137 MB vs 8 MB. SAME EXPERIMENT, SAME MACHINE, SAME AFTERNOON; ONLY THE INSTRUMENT CHANGED.
context: 2026-09-02, `DEF-109` third investigation pass (`PE-771`). `PE-769` had run the right experiment with an instrument that could not grade it, and had honestly recorded the result as neither confirmed nor refuted — which is why nothing false was published, but the pass cost a session and ended where it started. The third pass fixed the instrument BEFORE re-running anything, and the same intervention then produced an unambiguous verdict in two runs.
recommendation: Before running an experiment, write down what a negative result would mean under your instrument. If 'no change' is consistent with both 'my hypothesis is wrong' and 'my instrument cannot resolve this', the instrument is not yet good enough and the experiment is not worth running. Prefer the metric with a defined zero over the one that is merely available — retained bytes after a forced collection over working set, a row count over a process size, a captured artefact over a wall-clock duration. Then run the SAME instrument over baseline and intervention.
rationale: `LL-013`'s remedy protects against a scan with no subject; this protects against a scan whose subject is real but whose resolution is too coarse to answer the question. The failure is more dangerous because it produces a NUMBER rather than a silence, and a number that does not move reads as evidence of absence to everyone downstream. It is `LL-009`'s trap displaced by one step: there, two instruments agreeing were one instrument; here, one instrument answering was no instrument.
impact_if_followed: An experiment either produces a verdict that survives, or is not run — and the register never acquires a REFUTED that rests on an instrument's blindness, which is the entry that closes a live lead permanently and invisibly.
impact_if_ignored: A correct hypothesis is discarded on a null result the instrument could never have produced differently, and the investigation moves on with the door closed behind it. `DEF-056`'s vacuous control with the sign flipped: there a control passed over nothing, here a refutation rests on nothing.

title: A root-path tool names A path, never THE cause — and when the retention is structural, removing the suspect it names by name changes nothing, which is the tell that enumeration cannot terminate.
statement: SOS `gcroot` printed a path into a leaked object that ran through `DefaultPartitionedRateLimiter.RunTimer` — a named, plausible, project-owned suspect, sitting exactly where a cause belongs. REMOVING IT CHANGED NOTHING: 20 of 20 objects still rooted, retention 141 MB to 150 MB. Stripping every OpenTelemetry registration, the other named suspect, cut retention by a third and ALSO freed zero objects. The tool's own footer said what the path did not: `Found 505 unique roots`. THE STRUCTURE WAS THE CAUSE — an `ExecutionContext` captured during host startup, reachable from process-global state, so every long-lived thing started at startup roots the same graph and no single removal can end the enumeration. A path is a witness that the object is reachable; it is not a claim that it is reachable ONLY that way.
context: 2026-09-02, `DEF-109` third investigation pass (`PE-771`). The `gcroot` output was persuasive enough that writing 'the rate limiter's timer is the cause' straight off it would have felt like reading the answer rather than guessing it. Two bisects, each cheap, converted a persuasive path into a measured non-cause; the variable that actually isolated was the COUNT of hosts, which no root path mentions.
recommendation: Read the path-count before the path. If a rooting tool reports many unique roots, treat any single printed path as one witness among many and do not attribute cause to a name in it without removing that name and re-measuring. When two independent removals each fail to free the object, stop enumerating suspects and switch to varying the QUANTITY of the leaking unit — the number that changes retention is the diagnosis, and it will not appear in any root path.
rationale: The value of a root path is that it proves reachability and shows the mechanism's shape; its danger is that it hands you a specific, checkable-looking name at exactly the moment you want one. `LL-029` says only an intervention that isolates a variable explains — a printed path is a reading that FITS, which is the category `LL-029` exists to refuse, and it is unusually convincing because a tool produced it.
impact_if_followed: A named suspect is falsified in one cheap bisect instead of becoming the recorded cause, and the investigation reaches the structural variable rather than stopping one plausible name short of it.
impact_if_ignored: A defect row acquires a confident cause with a real stack path as its evidence, a remedy is built against it, and the remedy changes nothing — after which the row is harder to reopen than it was before, because it now reads as diagnosed.

title: A measurement that runs AFTER the action it should gate is a report, not a control — in a chained command the number prints, is correct, and changes nothing, and you read it only after the push has already happened.
statement: `LL-021` records that in `A && B && C` a failure in A stops the chain only for the commands that RUN. THE MIRROR IS WORSE AND FIRED HERE: A MEASUREMENT IN A CHAIN IS NOT A PREDICATE, SO IT STOPS NOTHING. Repairing a memory index that had exceeded its measured 200-line ceiling — a ceiling that exists because content past it is dropped SILENTLY — I wrote the trim, ran `wc -l`, and committed and pushed in the same `&&` chain. The count printed **202**. It was accurate, it was the exact number the whole edit existed to fix, and it was already in a pushed commit by the time I read it. **The violation I was correcting was reintroduced by the correction**, and it took two further pushes to land one trim. The fix is one construct: make the commit CONDITIONAL on the measurement — `LINES=$(wc -l < f); if [ "$LINES" -lt 200 ]; then git commit && git push; else echo OVER; fi` — at which point the same number that was a report becomes a gate.
context: 2026-09-02, close-out of the `DEF-109`/`DEC-112` session. The irony is load-bearing rather than decorative: the edit being committed was itself the repair of a limit violation, so the failure was not carelessness about the limit but a check placed downstream of the thing it was supposed to prevent. The third attempt used the conditional form and landed at 199 lines on the first try.
recommendation: Before chaining a check with an action, ask which one runs first. If the check's output is printed after the irreversible step — a commit, a push, a publish, an upsert — it is a report and must be rewritten as a predicate that can refuse. Where the action cannot be made conditional, split it into two invocations and read the number in between. ⚠ The tell is a command that ends `... && git commit && git push` with a `wc`, `grep -c`, or size check anywhere to its LEFT: the measurement has already been overtaken.
rationale: `LL-013` asks whether a check had a subject and `LL-041` whether its assertion had one; both assume the check is positioned to act. This is the prior failure: the check is correct, discriminating and about the right thing, and is simply downstream of the event it governs. It is more dangerous than a blind check because the number is RIGHT — the transcript shows the limit being measured and reported, which reads exactly like the limit being enforced, and a later reader auditing the session would see a measurement and conclude a control.
impact_if_followed: A bound is enforced by the same command that could violate it, so the violating state never reaches a commit — and a limit whose breach is silent never gets a chance to be silent.
impact_if_ignored: Irreversible steps ship over known-bad measurements, and the record shows the number being observed at the moment it was ignored. Worse in a repository where the breach is invisible: nothing downstream will ever contradict it.

title: Before filing a row's FIGURES as stale, ask whether a decision ruled that figure into place — `LL-038`'s question is about a status, and the same trap is set on a count.
statement: `LL-038` says: before repairing a row whose STATUS looks behind its evidence, ask whether the status is doing work. THE SAME TRAP IS SET ON A NUMBER, AND `LL-038`'s WORDING DOES NOT REACH IT. `DEF-087` asserts *"155 of 155 `wbs_items` have `slice_id` NULL"*; measured during a pre-interview sweep there are **187** items and **155** NULL, so the sentence reads plainly stale and a repair looked overdue. **`DEC-068` d2 had already ruled it**: `DEF-087` is fixed FORWARD only, the 155 historical rows are deliberately NOT backfilled, and — in the decision's own words — *"the defect row says so rather than being closed as repaired"*. **155 is not a rotted figure, it is the intended steady state**, and every row created since carries a `slice_id`, so the register is behaving exactly as ruled. Filing the repair would have reversed an operator decision while appearing to be routine hygiene.
context: 2026-09-02, the sweep before the `DEC-112` interview. The candidate was already drafted as a finding when the decision register was swept for the identifier; nothing in `DEF-087`'s own text names `DEC-068`, so only sweeping OUTWARD from the id found the ruling. The same sweep's other product was a real finding the agenda did not contain, so the pass both added and removed an item — and the removal is the half that never gets counted.
recommendation: When a row's stated count disagrees with the measured one, grep the DECISION, ADR, scope-change and open-question registers for that row's identifier BEFORE writing the finding. Ask what the number would be if the ruling had been obeyed perfectly — if that equals what you measured, the row is correct and the drift is in your reading. ⚠ A fix-forward ruling is the specific shape to watch: it deliberately freezes a historical figure while the total grows, so the row's number stays right while the ratio it appears in goes wrong.
rationale: A stale-looking number is the most inviting repair in a register: it is checkable, it looks mechanical, and fixing it feels like maintenance rather than a decision. That is exactly why it is dangerous — the repair reverses a ruling without ever presenting itself as a reversal, and no gate can object because both the old and the new number are internally consistent. `LL-025`'s shape (a row that quotes its requirement accurately can still be wrong because a decision superseded it), inverted: here the row is right and the reader's arithmetic is what is superseded.
impact_if_followed: A ruled figure is recognised as ruled, the sweep records a dissolved candidate rather than a defect, and the operator's decision survives a session that never intended to touch it.
impact_if_ignored: An operator decision is reversed as routine hygiene, in a commit whose message describes it as a correction — and because the new number is also true, nothing in the register will ever flag it.

title: The slate discipline guarantees the RECORDS you quote and nothing about the sentences you write around them — and an operator decision option is exactly such a sentence, carrying the same authority with none of the verification.
statement: `LL-011` and `gen-record-slate.mjs` exist so that every record put in front of the operator is byte-identical to the store, and the generator's own header already states the limit: *"the CONNECTIVE PROSE around these blocks is unguaranteed, and the TWENTY-SEVENTH reached the operator's decision slate through exactly that seam."* IT HAPPENED AGAIN, IN THE PLACE THE OPERATOR ACTUALLY READS. An `AskUserQuestion` option described a spike as *"take the .gdmp we still have locally"*, **the operator chose that option, and the file did not exist** — my own capture code had deleted it before upload for exceeding a ceiling I wrote, and I had quoted the manifest's `DROPPED ... (1253 MB)` line to the operator in the same conversation. **One `find` would have caught it and no gate ever will**, because a question's options are not a record and nothing reads them. ⚠ THE MECHANISM WAS SALIENCE, NOT IGNORANCE: I had spent an hour on that dump, and being vivid read as being present.
context: 2026-09-02, immediately after `DEC-115`. The four rulings in `DEC-115` itself were put against a generated slate whose nine blocks were verified byte-identical and were unaffected; the damaged ruling was a LATER, separate question whose options I wrote free-hand. The error surfaced only because the chosen option was then impossible to execute — had the spike been merely difficult rather than impossible, it would have stood.
recommendation: Treat every factual claim inside a question's options as an assertion that needs the same evidence as a claim inside a commit message. Before offering an option, run the command that would prove its premise — does the file exist, is the branch there, is the run still queryable — and prefer options phrased as capabilities you have just verified over ones phrased from recall. ⛔ The specific tell: a sentence containing *we still have*, *it is already there*, or *that is cheap* about an artefact you have not listed in this session.
rationale: The slate machinery makes the QUOTED half of a decision trustworthy, and that trustworthiness bleeds onto the unquoted half sitting beside it — the operator has no way to see which sentences were generated and which were typed. So the connective prose is not merely unguaranteed, it is guaranteed-looking, which is worse than obviously informal text would be. It is `LL-023`'s seam and it reopens whenever a question is composed rather than generated.
impact_if_followed: An operator rules on options whose premises were checked, so a chosen option is always executable — and the verified-block discipline extends to the words that frame them instead of stopping at their edge.
impact_if_ignored: A decision is made against a capability that does not exist, and it is discovered only when someone tries to act on it — or never, if the option was plausible enough to be quietly abandoned. The register then records a ruling whose basis was never true.
confirmed_by: Operator, 2026-09-02 (twenty-seventh round interview, DEC-116 d3) - approved, deliberately NOT pinned: it fires when an operator question is being composed, a narrower moment than the pinned set's every-session character (DEC-113 d3's split, applied again).

title: A file's NAME and its FIRST SCREEN both describe its format, never its content — and a capture manifest saying KEPT tells you nothing about what is inside the file it kept. Two sessions concluded evidence was locked in a dropped 1253 MB core dump while it sat in two files the capture had kept and uploaded.
statement: `DEF-121`'s crash artefact was declared insufficient twice, on two different files, by two different reading failures. `PE-784` described `info.log` as *"a binary-framed blob whose only matching content is that same crash record"* — it is a full system-state dump carrying `/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/cpuinfo`, mountinfo, a `ps` listing and the dpkg inventory. `PE-787` — itself written to correct `PE-784` for treating a zero-result grep as a read, and invoking `LL-041` and `LL-043` by name while doing it — then read the FIRST block of a 3,162-line `thread_information.log` (an `io` block, then a `sched` block), found scheduler statistics, and concluded the file held *"no thread state and no memory figure"*. The file is a REPEATING TRIPLE per thread and every third block is a full `/proc/<tid>/status`: 31 of them, each carrying `State:`, `VmRSS`, `VmHWM`, `VmSwap`, `VmPeak`. **The conclusion built on both readings — that the data able to test the memory-pressure hypothesis was inside the 1253 MB `.gdmp` the 64 MB ceiling dropped — was false, and the answer was in the uploaded artefact the whole time.** Read end to end, the two kept files refute that hypothesis outright: 214 MiB resident with the high-water mark equal to it, zero swap used by the process, and 10.7 GiB `MemAvailable` with 44 kB of 3 GiB swap in use on the host.
context: 2026-09-02, the session after `DEC-115`. `DEC-115` d2 had declined to chase the dropped dump and `DW-097` was `Activated` recording the gap as *"a 1253 MB dump requiring matching symbols"*. The next session's pre-interview sweep re-downloaded the artefact (still live, expires 2026-10-02) and read the two files rather than the entries about them, which dissolved the whole question — no ceiling change, no capture widening, and no specimen spike were needed. `PE-790` and `PE-791` are the corrections of record.
recommendation: Before recording what an artefact does or does not contain, READ IT END TO END, or state explicitly which part you read and scope the claim to that part. A structured log is very often a repeating multi-block record, so the first block is a sample of its FORMAT and not a census of its CONTENT — check the file's length against the size of the block you read before generalising. ⛔ The specific tell: a sentence of the form *"file X contains only Y"* where Y is what the first screen showed, or where the evidence is the file's NAME or its `file(1)` type. And when a capture manifest lists a file as `kept`, that is a statement about the copy succeeding, never about what is in it — the manifest can only be quoted for what was DROPPED.
rationale: A negative claim about a file's contents is a claim about every byte of it, and it is normally made from a sample: a grep pattern, the first screen, or the filename. Each of those can be wrong in the same direction — they all return *nothing of interest* when the interesting part is spelled differently, sits further down, or is inside a container format. `LL-041` covers the grep case and `LL-043` the spelling case; this is the third member and the one those two do not reach, because here the instrument was a HUMAN READ that simply stopped early. The cost is asymmetric and compounding: a false negative about an artefact does not merely omit evidence, it redirects work — here toward raising a ceiling, chasing a gigabyte dump, and inverting an operator's chosen ordering so that the verification would have required building the thing it was meant to justify.
impact_if_followed: Evidence already collected is actually used, and a capture's sufficiency is judged on what it contains rather than on what its manifest and filenames suggest — so an instrument is not widened, and a decision is not re-opened, to obtain something already in hand.
impact_if_ignored: A register accumulates confident negative statements about artefacts nobody read to the end, each of which redirects real work; and because a defect row's narrative is free text that no gate compares to the artefact it describes, the error is invisible until someone re-reads the file — which is exactly the state in which the wrong conclusion is durable.
confirmed_by: Operator, 2026-09-02 (twenty-seventh round interview, DEC-116 d3) - approved AND pinned: it fires before recording ANY claim about what an artefact contains, which is the pinned set's character.

title: A control chosen from INSIDE the scope you are searching confirms that boundary; it cannot test it. When the pattern is right and the corpus is right but the corpus is the WRONG ONE, a passing control makes the wrong answer feel measured.
statement: Asking which of eight carried defects had a RULING, I swept `decisions`, `adrs`, `open_questions`, `scope_changes` and `deferred_work`, and I calibrated it properly: the control `DEF-121` returned **15 naming rows**, so the scan demonstrably reached the corpus. Seven of eight were ruled and `DEF-101` was named by nothing — a clean, evidenced, **wrong** answer. `DEF-101` was dispositioned by the operator on 2026-08-20 and the ruling lives in `PE-565`: *"the operator chose to leave the honest gap... I offered to reconstruct it and the refusal is the more disciplined answer"*. **Progress entries were not in the swept scope, and `DEF-121` could never have revealed that, because I picked it from inside the scope I was already searching.** It was a good control for *did the scan run* and a worthless one for *is this the right corpus* — the two questions look identical from the passing side.
context: 2026-09-02, a register-liveness pass on the `defects-minor` advisory, whose own note is *carrying them is legal, silence is not*. Caught before it reached the operator, and only because I read the other seventeen rows citing `DEF-082` instead of counting them: fifteen were later sessions repeating *"the exception is DEF-082, which DEF-101 records"*, and two were the ruling. `PE-806` is the record.
recommendation: Choose the control from the scope you might be MISSING, never from the scope you are searching. Before running a *does any row say X* sweep, name one row you believe is OUTSIDE your file list and confirm the sweep fails to find it — a control that cannot fail is not a control. ⛔ For *what was decided* in this package specifically, the scope is `decisions` + `adrs` + `open_questions` + `scope_changes` + `deferred_work` + **`progress_entries`**, and defect rows too (`LL-040`). ⚠ The tell: a negative result about the whole register produced by a file list you chose without justifying its completeness.
rationale: `LL-013` asks whether the scanner looked at anything and `LL-033` asks whether the pattern matches the corpus's spelling of the concept. This is the third member and neither reaches it: here the pattern was exact, the corpus was real, the control passed honestly, and the boundary was drawn one register short. **A calibration establishes that the instrument works within the frame; it says nothing about the frame.** That is why the failure feels like a measurement rather than an oversight — every step of it was rigorous except the one nobody wrote down, which was the choice of file list. `LL-040` already named this in one direction (a ruling can sit in a closed defect row) and the standing note names it in another (a progress entry is a ruling's record too); what neither supplies is the mechanical guard, which is a control that lives outside the boundary.
impact_if_followed: A negative sweep result is trustworthy about the whole register rather than about an unstated subset, so an operator is never told a row is unruled when their own ruling is on the record.
impact_if_ignored: Agents re-open settled questions with evidence that looks measured, which is worse than re-opening them on a hunch: the passing control makes the wrong answer hard to argue with, and the operator is asked to rule a second time on something they already decided — which `LL-002` costs, and which erodes trust in the sweep habit that is otherwise this project's most productive one.

title: A TRIGGER THAT NEVER FIRES, ONE THAT ALWAYS FIRES, AND ONE WHOSE SILENCE YOU CANNOT READ ARE THE SAME FAULT — nobody measured how often it fires, or proved it runs where it matters. The later members are worse, because they produce output.
statement: `WBS-27.1` built an instrument for `DEF-109` precisely because that row's clause (2) COULD NOT FIRE. Its own trigger was then wrong in THREE ways within one day. **(1) It could never fire:** `availableWorkers == 0` counts against the pool MAXIMUM of 32767, so it needed 32,767 concurrent work items — dead code, caught only in review. **(2) Corrected, it fired on its FIRST CI run during an ordinary passing suite**, because a queued work item at the instant of sampling is routine on a loaded 4-core runner and never happened on an idle 24-core local box; it turned `main` red. **(3) Repaired again, it then wrote NOTHING during `DEF-109` occurrence 5** — 24 m 34 s, 38 failures, 37 requests each burning a 100-second ceiling. Both upload steps ran and found no files. ⛔ **That silence is unreadable, because an empty artefact is produced identically by *it ran and saw nothing* and by *it never ran*, and the instrument shipped no positive control.**
context: 2026-09-03, `WBS-27.1` (`DEC-120` d3), across PRs `#342` and `#343` and `DEF-109` occurrence 5 on CI run `33732803634`. Members (1) and (2) are `PE-816`; member (3) is `PE-817` and `DEF-131`. `DEC-121` d4 confirmed the three as one lesson rather than separate rows.
recommendation: Before shipping any detector, answer three questions and write the answers down. **(a) CAN it fire at all?** Compute the extreme — `GetAvailableThreads` counts against the pool MAX, not the live worker count. **(b) How often does it fire on a NORMAL run?** If the answer is *every time*, it is not a detector, it is a log line. **(c) Can you tell its SILENCE apart from its ABSENCE?** If not, add a positive control so the artefact's EXISTENCE proves the detector ran and its CONTENT carries the finding. ⭐ This project already does (c) four times — `DW-068`, `DW-084`, `AV-213`, `AV-216` — and records it in no rule register, so it is learnable only by having read those rows. ⛔ Where a normal rate has never been measured, prefer a SUSTAINED condition over an invented threshold, and calibrate the threshold only AFTER the control proves the detector is live — never from the same run that first raised the doubt.
rationale:
`DEF-078` and `LL-013` cover member (1) — a green control with no subject, and proving the scanner looked at something. **Neither reaches (2) or (3), and that is what this adds.** A detector that fires on every run PASSES every calibration those lessons prescribe: it demonstrably ran, demonstrably emitted, and demonstrably responds to an injected fault. It is broken anyway, because a signal present in every sample carries no information — and unlike silence, its output actively reassures.
⭐⭐ **MEMBER (3) IS THE SHARPEST AND IS A RULE `LL-013` DOES NOT STATE: A CALIBRATION IN THE TEST ENVIRONMENT PROVES THE MECHANISM, NEVER THE DEPLOYMENT.** `StallWatchdogTests` is 10 of 10 green and mutation-checked TWICE, and the `[ModuleInitializer]` that starts the sampling thread on a CI runner is exercised by no test at all — so the instrument may be perfect and still never have run where it was needed. `AV-216`'s *"CONFIRMED LIVE, not only by source reading"* had gestured at this four rows earlier without ever stating it as a rule.
⚠ **AND THE FAILURE MODES GET HARDER TO SEE IN ORDER.** (1) failed loudly in review. (2) failed loudly in CI. **(3) does not fail at all — it returns a clean, quiet, plausible absence that reads exactly like a result**, which is why it was the one that needed an interview rather than a fix.
impact_if_followed: A detector's first real run either confirms an estimate that was written down or contradicts it, and its silence is always interpretable — so an over-sensitive trigger is caught before its artefact teaches anyone to ignore it, and a dead one is caught before its quiet is mistaken for a finding.
impact_if_ignored: Detectors accumulate that pass every check this project runs — they execute, they emit, they respond to injected faults — while carrying no information; and worse, an absence they produce gets read as evidence, so an investigation draws a confident conclusion from an instrument that may never have started.
confirmed_by: Operator, 2026-09-03 (thirty-second round interview, DEC-121 d4) — approved AND pinned, with the third member folded in rather than given its own row (LL-016)

title: A positive control proves the instrument FIRES. It cannot prove the trigger's SUBJECT is the fault's SYMPTOM — so when you identify that unmeasured step and defer it, ask whether a cheaper injection exists, because that step decides whether the instrument works at all.
statement:
`LL-013` says prove the scanner looked at something. `LL-047` says ask what a NEGATIVE result would mean. `DEF-131` added: make the artefact's EXISTENCE prove the instrument ran. **ALL THREE WERE SATISFIED, TO THE LETTER, BY AN INSTRUMENT THAT COULD NOT OBSERVE ITS FAULT.** `WBS-27.1`'s stall watchdog exists to make `DEF-109`'s clause (2) reachable. Its sole trigger fires when a dedicated sampler asks to sleep 5 s and wakes ≥20 s later - a measure of the PROCESS not being scheduled. `StallWatchdogTests` injects a 40-second drift and watches a snapshot appear: 10 of 10 green, mutation-checked twice, `CaptureIfDegraded` made `internal` specifically so that control could exist. **Then the fault fired for real.** Occurrence 6: eighteen requests each burned a full 100-second `HttpClient` ceiling across seventeen classes over 17 minutes, and `windowMaxDrift` was **0.049 s once and under 3 MILLISECONDS in every other window** against a 15-second threshold. **The process was scheduled promptly throughout the failure, so the trigger's quantity never left its healthy value and no threshold on it could ever have fired.**
✅ **AND THE PART THAT MAKES THIS A LESSON RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT: THE GAP WAS DECLARED IN ADVANCE.** That test file's header states it before any test - *"they prove nothing about whether a real `DEF-109` occurrence produces a large drift. Only an occurrence can show that."* **The step was identified, written down, and consciously deferred**, which is `DW-097`'s falsifiable-instrument model working; the instrument was falsified on its first firing exactly as designed. ⛔ **BUT A CHEAPER INJECTION EXISTED THE WHOLE TIME.** The fault's symptom is a request hung past its ceiling, and a request-in-flight register is injectable in-process with no occurrence required - it would have shown before merge that the trigger's quantity does not move. **The deferral was reasonable and it cost two days and three PRs, because the declared-but-unmeasured step was the one that decided whether the instrument worked at all.**
context: 2026-09-03, `DEF-109` occurrence 6 (`PE-829`), the first occurrence of that defect ever to leave an artefact. Three PRs across two days built the instrument (`#342`), fixed a test of its own (`#343`) and gave it a positive control (`#344`), and `DEC-121` d3 ruled the ORDER: control first, threshold calibrated only afterwards from real data. The artefact did real work - it refuted thread-pool starvation, half of what `DEC-110` d2 named as the investigation target, on 204 samples of direct evidence - and it did so through its HEARTBEAT, not its trigger, which recorded nothing on the one run it was built for. Filed as `DEF-134`; `DEC-125` d1 retargets the trigger at the fault's own symptom and adds thread/task state. ⚠ The first draft of this lesson said the coupling had been overlooked; it had been declared, and `PE-830` is the correction.
recommendation: Write down the causal chain from the FAULT to the quantity your trigger reads, and name the step you have not measured - most instruments here already do this well. **Then, before deferring that step to *only a real occurrence can show it*, spend five minutes asking whether a cheaper injection reaches it.** Prefer a trigger keyed on the fault's own definition over a proxy that is merely easier to sample, because a seam at the fault's definition is usually the seam that makes the coupling injectable too. Where the step genuinely cannot be closed before shipping, put it in the ARTEFACT's header as well as the test's, so the reader who downloads it weeks later can tell a silence that refutes from a silence that could not have spoken.
rationale: `LL-013`, `LL-047` and `DEF-131` all guard the instrument's relationship to ITSELF - did it run, could its negative mean anything, does its output prove it was alive. **None of them reaches the instrument's relationship to the FAULT**, and that gap is invisible from inside a test suite, which can only inject what the code under test accepts. It is `LL-009`'s trap displaced one step further than `LL-047` displaced it: there, two instruments agreeing were one instrument; in `LL-047`, one instrument answering was no instrument; here, an instrument that verifiably fires is pointed at the wrong quantity. ⚠ It is also `LL-054`'s fourth member with a new mechanism - that lesson's members were a predicate that could never fire, one that always fired, and a calibration proving the mechanism rather than the deployment. **This one fires correctly on its own subject, where the subject is not the fault** - and unlike the first three it fails SILENTLY and looks like a result. ⭐ The distinctive half is that good practice was followed and was not sufficient: the limit was declared, the instrument was falsifiable, and it was duly falsified - two days later, by an intermittent fault, when a five-minute in-process injection would have done it before merge.
impact_if_followed: The path from fault to trigger is exercised before a detector ships wherever a cheap injection reaches it, so a detector's silence on a real occurrence is a finding about the fault rather than a fact about its own design - and clause-style end conditions that depend on a capture stop being satisfiable in form while unreachable in substance.
impact_if_ignored: An instrument accumulates artefacts that read as evidence and are facts about its own trigger, and each new occurrence re-reads the same silence as fresh confirmation. Worse than `DEF-078`'s green control with no subject, because there the control was empty; here it is full, careful, honest about its limits, and about something else. `DEF-134` is the instance: three PRs and two days made `DEF-109`'s clause (2) reachable in FORM while leaving it unreachable in SUBSTANCE, and the artefact's arrival made that harder to notice rather than easier.

title: A local document's EXAMPLES are its measured cases; its stated MECHANISM is an extrapolation over them. The advice can be right while the reason is false — and the reason is what you generalise from the moment you meet a case the examples do not list.
statement:
`.claude/PERMISSIONS.md` and `permission-prompts-four-causes.md` both explained permission prompts with: *"the matcher matches the FIRST TOKEN of the whole command string, so anything that is not the allowed leader defeats it"*, over a table of three costumes — a `cd` prefix, a leading variable assignment, a pipe. **All three costumes are real. Every recommendation drawn from them is right.** ⛔ **THE SENTENCE EXPLAINING THEM IS FALSE.** The official documentation says Claude Code splits on `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|`, `|&`, `&` and newlines and that **a rule must match each subcommand independently** — and, separately, that a `cd` inside the working directory is itself read-only, so `cd packages/api && ls` is documented as prompting-free.
⛔⛔ **THE FALSE MECHANISM DID NOT MIS-EXPLAIN THE PAST; IT MIS-PREDICTED THE FUTURE, WITHIN THE HOUR.** Reasoning from FIRST-TOKEN I ran `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process … | Select-Object … | Format-List` and put it in a table for the operator marked **ALLOWED**, because its leader is allowlisted and the leader is what the model says decides. It prompted. `Select-Object` and `Format-List` have no rule in either settings file — **under the true model the prompt was derivable before the command was sent.** The mirror error is as costly: FIRST-TOKEN says every pipeline is unmatchable, so it also forbids `grep … | sort | tail`, which is in fact free.
⭐⭐ **THE STRUCTURAL POINT: THE THREE COSTUMES WERE OBSERVATIONS AND THE MECHANISM WAS THE FIT THROUGH THEM.** A wrong curve through three correct points reproduces all three. **It only diverges on the fourth**, and the fourth is exactly the case you consult the document about — nobody re-reads a document for a case it already lists.
context: 2026-09-04, opening a session on `prm-next.md`. The operator interrupted with *"I cannot accept this, you still ask for permissions"*. I built a per-command table from `PERMISSIONS.md`'s model and presented it as **measured** — it was the document's model applied to my transcript, which is the same fault as the *fifth permission cause* retracted the previous day (`PE-834`). The operator then said to check the official documentation first and the advisor second; the docs refuted the mechanism, and asking the operator directly which dialogs appeared returned **all four** of my candidates — including the pipeline I had scored as allowed and the `cd` chains the docs say should be free. Filed as `DEF-135`; `DEF-133` (the same file's `node -e` recommendation) was fixed in the same edit.
recommendation: When a local document explains WHY a tool behaves as it does, treat its examples and its explanation as two different grades of evidence. **Use the examples; verify the explanation against the vendor's own documentation before extrapolating from it** — and the trigger for doing so is precise: *you are about to apply the rule to a case the document's table does not contain.* ⭐ For anything whose evidence is a dialog, a colour, or any signal that never reaches a tool result, **ask the operator which one they saw before building the explanation.** One question settled this in a word after two sessions of inference, exactly as it did the previous time.
rationale: `LL-006` says read the implementation, not the document describing it — but here **both sources were documents and they agreed with each other**, so there was no disagreement to notice; the discriminator was a third source, the vendor's, that neither contained. It is not the FORTY-FIFTH's class either: that was a TRUE claim under a stale INSTRUCTION, this is a FALSE claim under a live and correct instruction — opposite halves, and this one is worse because a reviewer checks the instruction and passes. ⚠ It is `LL-055`'s neighbour rather than `LL-055`: that lesson is about verifying a premise on one part and assuming it across the rest; **this is about a premise verified on every part it names, and extrapolated past them.** ⛔ No instrument here can see it: no gate reads prose, `count-prompt-ids.py` resolves identifiers, and the file's own recommendations — which any review would check — were all correct.
impact_if_followed: A local operations document keeps its authority where it is strongest (the cases it actually measured) and stops being used as a model of the tool. Extrapolations get checked against the vendor at the one moment they matter — the unlisted case — which is cheap, because that moment is rare and self-announcing.
impact_if_ignored: The document accumulates correct advice around a wrong reason, and every reader who meets a new case derives the wrong answer from it with full confidence and no way to notice — here, twice in two days on the same file, the second time inside a table labelled *measured* and shown to the operator as evidence. ⚠ And because the advice keeps working, each failure reads as a fresh mystery rather than as the same fault, which is what makes it survive a review.
